Application orchestration is now separated from native transaction
synthesis. The replacement adapters and central dispatcher moved from
`src/app/main.cpp` behind the single public
`app/native_replacements.hpp` entry point. `main.cpp` fell from 16,939
lines/630 KB to 5,077 lines while retaining command-line, recording, replay,
cabinet, and runtime ownership. Collision, physics/arithmetic,
controls/actor, and rules/RNG/score synthesis now occupy four subsystem
implementation units behind a private internal interface;
`native_replacements.cpp` is the 555-line central registry. The extracted
modules have no SDL, cabinet, recording-plan, or replay-capture dependency,
and `main.cpp` no longer includes the game-logic C headers directly.

Work has moved off the unusually large collision-table interpreter.
Semantic `00:F1B4@all` now derives position-integration sign branches,
comparison exits, flags, writes, and timing from live slot-zero state,
executing all 1,156 calls through path-sensitive 50-57-boundary transcripts,
including 250 original interrupt-bearing scopes. The adjacent state-generic
`00:F241@all` rollback executes all 404 calls through a 12-boundary
transcript. The complete 1,560-call position pipeline is native while both
routines retain exact gameplay and complete call/write artifacts.

Semantic `03:7FB1@all` now replaces the actor collision-response helper by
live slot state rather than ordinal. It derives response, countdown,
reload/phase advancement, result flags, three-or-five-write transcript, and
126/162-cycle timing for any slot. Its 11/14-boundary transcripts now admit
all 21,987 calls, including 1,042 calls with original interrupt-handler
passages; the state census and complete 21,987-call/91,295-write artifacts
remain byte-identical in Debug and Release.

Semantic `03:7F57@all` now composes those collision primitives at the
Small-Soldier consumer boundary. For a live no-hit state it invokes any
admitted semantic `03:6966` transaction, stages those writes into a private
snapshot, invokes either semantic `03:7FB1` branch from the resulting state,
and finally reproduces the caller's collision-byte test. Write offsets and
body timing are derived from the two child transactions without an ordinal
table. The alternate-pass, one-axis, and bounded two-axis headerless shapes
compose their children's checkpoints with both parent JSR/RTS boundaries
and the final collision test, producing 35/38-, 68/71-, or
73/76-boundary parent transcripts. This admits 20,113 of 20,867 calls
(96.4%); the complete
20,867-call/362,060-write artifacts remain byte-identical in Debug and
Release.

The downstream HuC6280 bridge now supports optional resumable replacement
transcripts. It commits ordered writes only as their checkpoints are reached,
samples IRQ state at the original instruction's last-cycle boundary, and
serializes pending writes/checkpoints in savestates. If an interrupt handler
returns without restoring the expected registers or MPRs, Beetle abandons the
remaining transcript at that original instruction and continues in assembly.
Atomic replacements without checkpoints retain their conservative event/IRQ
horizon policy.

No whole-project percentage is reported yet. The remaining milestones have
not been decomposed finely enough for a single aggregate number to be useful.

### Milestone 2 closure checklist

Milestone 2 no longer uses a percentage estimate. The previous weighted
estimate mixed completed architecture work with an expanding set of
reverse-engineering discoveries, so its denominator was not stable. The
milestone closes when these four evidence-based gates are complete:

| Gate | Existing evidence | Required closure evidence | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Normal-table controls and physics | One 3,600-frame route connects Button-I Devil-Shooter charge/release, right/left flipper state changes, and three Button-II nudges to slot-0 motion and later integration; `$2CC7` remains clear throughout | Deterministic combined route, ROM gates, complete work-RAM timeline, ordered calls, and selected writes are guarded by `dc_rom_controls_physics` | Closed |
| Normal-table collision boundary | Natural Small-Soldier contacts at frames 1,479 and 1,852 connect `01:CBCF` and the type-`$82` ball response through `03:6966`/`03:7FB1` to actor state, score, command `$21`, `$2D16`, and complete actor release | ROM gates, complete work-RAM timeline, 97,379 ordered calls, 1,163,259 scoped writes, and selected state writes are guarded by `dc_rom_collision_boundary` | Closed |
| Normal-table session and scoring boundary | One route connects the frame-3,000 live-ball drain, `$2D52` decrement, ordinary continuation decision, category-1 reload, 1,020-unit stored score, dirty-panel handoff, and remaining-ball redraw | ROM gates, complete work-RAM timeline, 402 ordered calls, 27,769 scoped writes, and exact score/ball glyph streams are guarded by `dc_rom_session_scoring` | Closed |
| Coverage manifest and scope freeze | `docs/COVERAGE_MANIFEST.md` contains 105 unique classified behavior units: 57 dynamic, 29 static, and 19 deferred | `dc_coverage_manifest` guards unique IDs, the complete manual audit, classification totals, and registered evidence tests | Closed |

The instrumentation registry, trace and replay support, transactional
no-interrupt native boundary, shadow comparison, and faithful replacement of
`00:F241@1` already satisfy the Milestone 2 bridge proof. Every bonus stage
already has a bounded event family, timeout, completion, ordinary
scored-but-incomplete result, and perfect result; further outcome variants do
not block closure.

### Milestone 2 scope boundary

The following work is explicitly deferred and must not reopen Milestone 2:

- Exhaustive dynamic reproduction of every statically mapped normal-table
  mechanism branch. Exercise each family during Milestone 4 as its routines
  are observed, shadow-tested, and replaced.
- Additional bonus-stage event families and redundant success, perfect,
  failure, or timeout variants beyond the bounded baseline. Add them during
  the corresponding Milestone 4 port or Milestone 6 acceptance pass.
- Faithful mid-routine interrupt delivery was deferred from Milestone 2 and
  completed in Milestone 4 on 2026-07-29. Semantic `01:D081@all` is the first
  interrupt-bearing proof, with all 540 calls preserving exact artifacts.
- Exhaustive combinations of both speeds, both player counts, every drain,
  extra-ball, last-chance, and stuck-ball variant. These remain release
  acceptance requirements, not prerequisites for closing the instrumentation
  milestone.

| 5. Final cabinet world model | Not started | Desktop and cabinet profiles share the same native gameplay state without divergence |

  to the port. `VCE::FrameDone` is written by `StartFrame` and `RunPartial`
  and by nothing else -- neither the constructor nor `Reset` touches it -- so
  before the first `StartFrame` the emulator's flag is whatever its allocation
  held. Release reads zero from a fresh page and agrees by accident; Debug
  reads the CRT's fill pattern and does not. The machine is not disagreeing:
  nothing reads the flag before `StartFrame`, because `Emulate` calls it
  first. The test was over-specifying, and now compares that field only once a
  frame has started.

    on every launch.

    walk that inlined a call ending at any of them fell through to `default`

    refusals, six times every other cause in the bank put together.**

    is conditional on the mask actually being open, which is what keeps it
    cheap -- reached already masked, the deferred byte and the true byte are
    the same byte.

    exempted the whole body from its own staleness test on the strength of one
    byte it was handed on the way in.

### Previous: the score panel's redraw poll

**The largest thing left in bank `09` had never been ranked, and the reason is
worth more than the routine.** The candidate analyzer groups *contiguous
executed* addresses into approximate routines. `09:7237` branches forward over a
countdown this route never takes, at `7249`-`725B`, so the profile has a hole in
the middle of it and the analyzer offered two runs instead: `09:71EA`-`7247`,
which ends in the middle of the poll and begins in the middle of an unrelated
animation stepper, and `09:725E`-`72EA`, which begins at the poll's own join
point. `### Next` carried both as separate recommendations. Neither is a
routine. Read as one, they are ten instructions and **327,924 master cycles,
forty-two per cent of what the previous slice left in the bank** -- more than
either fragment and more than anything else in it.

**What it does is decide not to work.** Four gates, all read straight out of
work RAM: the redraw-in-progress flag `$2DBB`, the session handshake `$2D53`,
the hold-off countdown `$2D70`, and bit 0 of `$2CC0`. That last one is the panel
dirty bit -- `00:F55C`'s score accumulator sets it, `01:C812` sets it again when
a ball is lost, and `ROUTINE_MAP.md` has recorded the far side of this poll for
several milestones as "`09:7266`, `09:72FD`: consumes the dirty bit and redraws
the score and remaining-ball digits". So the addresses named the routine before
the control flow did, again. On the census route it returns without doing
anything 2,616 times out of 2,649.

The walk is state-generic and ends wherever the gates send it: `$2DBB` non-zero
stops in front of the `JMP` at `723C`, `$2D70` non-zero stops in front of the
`DEC` at `7249`, and the dirty bit set walks the two work RAM instructions that
consume the request before handing back the redraw itself, which is where the
VDC traffic is. The `$2D53` arm needs no code at all -- it branches to `725E`,
which the walk models for every call anyway. Only the common answer absorbs the
`RTS`.

**`BIT #$01` is the instruction that had to come out of the core rather than the
datasheet.** A 65C02's immediate-mode `BIT` is the documented exception that
affects only `Z`; this core has a single `BIT` macro shared across every
addressing mode, so `BIT #$01` also clears `N` and `V` from the operand's top two
bits. Implementing the documented behaviour would not have corrupted anything --
the host compares registers at each resume point -- but it would have abandoned
the transcript on all 2,649 calls while the deployment line went on saying 433
of 433. The number that moves in that case is `Registry abandonments`, and it is
easy to read past.

| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Emulated in `09:7237`-`7265` | 327,924 | **0** |
| Registry cycles | 694,772,727 | **695,098,752** |
| Native share | 53.76% | **53.78%** |
| Native share outside the wait | 97.79% | **97.83%** |
| Admitted routines | 432 | **433** |
| Routines entered | 365 | **366** |
| Bank `09` outside the wait | 782,010 | **453,369** |
| Release tests | 424 | **425** |

The registry gained 326,025, which is the transcripts' modelled cycles exactly:
2,649 x 102 for the gates, 2,616 x 21 for the absorbed `RTS`, 33 x 27 for the
taken branch and the two instructions that consume the request. The bank's
emulated remainder fell by 2,616 more than that, and the difference is the
per-row interrupt overhang the profile charges to whichever instruction was
executing -- a fixed error on ten addresses, not a discrepancy.

**A routine whose product is a decision needs an oracle for the decision.** This
one writes a single byte, thirty-three times in 3,600 frames. The write-range
comparison this project uses everywhere would have been nearly empty here, and
would have passed just as happily with the wrong `N` and `V` on the 2,616 calls
that write nothing at all -- which, given the `BIT` above, was the live risk and
not a hypothetical one. So the primary artifact is the **routine-call trace**,
compared emulated against replaced: it carries `output_a`, `output_status`,
`body_master_cycles` and `return_instruction_pc` for every call, so it compares
the arm the gates chose and the flags the walk left, and it is also what proves
the absorbed `RTS` put the observer's boundary back. `return_instruction_pc`
splits 2,616 at `7265` and 33 at `72EA`, and a gate read from the wrong address
moves that split before it moves anything else.

Three write channels sit under it, chosen for what the decision *enables* rather
than for what the routine writes: `$202D`-`$2036`, the zero-page scratch the
redraw builds its VRAM cursor in and which stays empty unless the gate opens;

whole visible output is a tile stream through those four registers and a dirty
bit consumed one call early or late would move it. A work-RAM census cannot see
a device write at all.

### Previous: bank `01`'s jump table
`01:C000`-`01:C0CB` is sixty-eight `JMP absolute` rows, three bytes each, and it
is how the rest of the cartridge reaches bank 01's routines -- and, through the
bank-call wrapper at `00:E241`, bank 00's. A caller names a row rather than a
routine, which is why the table exists and why nothing in the port had touched
it: it is not a routine, it is a switchboard.
`01:C000`-`01:C0CB` is sixty-eight `JMP absolute` rows, three bytes each, and it
is how the rest of the cartridge reaches bank 01's routines -- and, through the
bank-call wrapper at `00:E241`, bank 00's. A caller names a row rather than a
routine, which is why the table exists and why nothing in the port had touched
it: it is not a routine, it is a switchboard.

Eighteen rows execute on this route, 8,541 arrivals between them:

| Row | Target | Row | Target | Row | Target |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `C012` | `$F08E` | `C03C` | `$E93C` | `C06C` | `$F4FC` |
| `C018` | `$C5C9` | `C042` | `$E1FD` | `C06F` | `$DAF8` |
| `C021` | `$C5EA` | `C05D` | `$EBA5` | `C081` | `$E8B3` |
| `C024` | `$C5AB` | `C060` | `$E241` | `C087` | `$ECFD` |
| `C027` | `$C574` | `C063` | `$D6E2` | `C09F` | `$D8CA` |
| `C02A` | `$F54F` | `C069` | `$D75E` | `C0A2` | `$D8D2` |

**This is the shortest transcript the port can write, and the only one whose
correctness is settled by the ROM alone.** `JMP absolute` reads two operand
bytes, sets the program counter, and charges `ADDCYC(3)` plus the `LastCycle`:
no flag moves, no register moves, nothing is read from work RAM and nothing is
written to it. Every other family in this port has to argue that the state it
read is the state the route will always present. This one does not have state.
The two operand bytes come through MPR6, and a transaction admitted at
`01:C0xx` *is* the statement that MPR6 holds bank 01 -- so the bytes are bank
01's own `$0012`, `$0018` and so on, and the target beside each row above is
the disassembly's rather than a guess.

Each walk ends on its target, the same way a crossed `JSR` ends on its callee's
first instruction and for the same reason: the transcript did the transfer, and
whatever owns the address on the far side picks the body up. Eleven of the
eighteen targets are registered entries and continue natively; the other seven
hand back to the interpreter, which costs nothing. **A row is not a claim about
the routine it names.**

The single checkpoint is not decoration. The profile shows interrupts landing on
these instructions -- `01:C012`'s 924 arrivals cost 11,160 rather than 11,088 --
and the checkpoint is where the core samples for one, at the `LastCycle`,
exactly as the assembly does.

**A pinned relic was retired, and the measurement that retired it is the best
thing in this slice.** `01:C024` was already owned --

identical to this one but gated on `A=$42, X=$3A, Y=0, SP=$F4, P=0`, admitted

proved itself by reproducing one observed state. A `JMP` has no state to be
generic about, so the general row simply subsumes it; the function and its
dispatch are deleted. Running all sixty-four arrivals natively instead of one

more native arrivals, and not one byte of the machine moved. The generator's
partial-coverage count fell 88 to 87.

**The oracle is the stack page, because this family writes nothing of its own.**
There is no output range to compare: a row moves the program counter and charges
twelve cycles, and that is all of it. But a cycle miscounted here shifts every
later instruction on the route, and `$2100-21FF` carries the cycle of every push
and pop the route makes. So the regression records the route twice, emulated and
replaced, over the stack page, and requires the traces to be identical --
4,205,699 writes, same bytes, same order, same cycles. A row priced at eleven or
thirteen would move the whole trace from that point on. The census is pinned on
top, because a comparison cannot see route drift and because a wrong *target*
would not shift the stack page, it would end the route. 32.2s.

**Fifty rows are handed back for want of a witness**, and nothing about them is

One number in this file needed correcting: the recommendation priced this slice

### Previous: the main session loop
`01:C154`-`01:C1B5` is the loop the whole game runs in -- wait for the frame,
call the nine things a frame is made of, ask whether to run another -- and it
was 1,259,148 emulated master cycles, the fourth-largest run left outside the
frame-sync wait and the largest that was actually work.

**It ports as a chain of crossings, not as a walk.** A transcript that makes a
call ends on it, so the loop is ten transcripts rather than one, each entered at
the address the previous callee returns to:

```
C157 C15A C15D C166 C169 C16C C16F C17A C185 C190
```

Composition -- splicing the callee's transcript in and walking its `RTS` back,
which is what the collision sweep does one level down -- is not available here.
These callees are the frame's entire actor scan and motion pass: tens of
thousands of cycles and hundreds of writes each, past every interrupt horizon
and both channel caps. Crossing is the only shape that fits, and it is enough,
because eight of the nine calls land on a transcript this port already owns.

**The frame-sync wait is crossed too, and it is not a porting target.** The
ninth call is `00:E321`, where the machine is *meant* to sit; the note this
file left last slice said the walk hands over there, and handing over was one
cycle-count too pessimistic. A crossing does not port the callee -- it makes the
`JSR` itself, 21 master cycles, and hands the interpreter the callee's first
instruction. So the walk entered at `01:C190` runs the whole tail and the call
at `01:C154`, and the interpreter picks up in the spin exactly as before.

| | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Emulated in `01:C154`-`01:C1B5` | 1,259,148 | **21** |
| Registry cycles | 692,715,369 | **693,963,048** |
| Native share | 53.60% | **53.70%** |
| Native share outside the wait | 97.50% | **97.67%** |
| Admitted routines | 404 | **414** |
| Registry calls | 2,713,488 | **2,739,978** |
| Release tests | 421 | **422** |

Twenty-one cycles is one `JSR $E321` executed once, at start-up, by falling
through from `01:C151`. `01:C154` is deliberately not an entry: every other
arrival at it comes from inside the walk that crosses it.

**`BIT #` sets N and V on this core.** A 65C02 leaves both alone for the
immediate form. The core routes every addressing mode of `BIT` through one
macro -- `P &= ~(Z|V|N); P |= ZNTable[x & A] & Z; P |= x & (V|N);` -- so the
four tail tests set N from `#$80` and V from `#$40`, out of the operand rather
than the result. Nothing in the loop reads either flag; all four branch on Z.
The transcript carries them anyway, for the same reason the `JSR` pushes moved
last slice: **a transcript states what the emulator would have done, and where
the emulator and the processor differ the emulator wins by definition.**

**Six arms are handed back and one of them is live.** `01:C1A2`, `01:C1A9`,
`01:C1B0`, `01:C1B7` and `01:C1BA` are the five ways the session leaves the
loop, and `01:C195` is the maximum-score ending. None executes on this route,
so transcribing one would be claiming a path this port has never watched run --
and `01:C195` really is reached in play, because the score-saturation helper
sets `$2CC0.7` and the ending goes through it.

**The guard built last slice paid for itself on its first use.** Ten crossings
are twenty stack pushes an iteration, which is the exact defect class that has
now appeared three times, and `dc_rom_registry_stack_page_writes` compares the
whole route's writes to `$2100-21FF` against pure assembly. All 4,205,699 still
match, hash unchanged at `6b1d9dea…`. Nothing else in the suite would have
looked.

The new regression is a comparison for the same reason, not a digest: it records
the route twice, emulated and replaced, over the two request bytes at
`$202F`-`$2030`, and requires the traces to be identical -- 1,169,947 writes,
same values, same order, same cycles. The census is pinned on top of that,
because a comparison cannot see route drift; both sides would drift together.
21.5s.

**`--observe-hook` cannot be used on an address that is not a routine head**,
which cost an hour to learn. The first attempt at this regression used the usual
observe-plus-call-trace shape and died at frame 1,240. It is not a replacement
fault: with *no* replacement installed and three observe hooks on these
addresses, the recorder reached 79 GB by half the route. An observed call is
closed by its return, and these entries are return addresses -- the call never
closes. The write-trace shape has no such problem and is the right oracle here
anyway.

`windows-debug` was not run.

### Previous: the six cycles under `01:C018`
Done, and the heading is wrong: nothing was under `01:C018`. The finding named the
`JSR $C018` that preceded the two mis-declared writes because that is what a
reader's eye lands on, and the actual fault was the instruction *after* it, in
a transcript that had been deployed and passing for months.

**Both addresses were the entry instruction of their own replacement.**
`02:53C8` is `JSR $53E4` and `02:5441` is `JSR $545D` -- the heads of the
Devil-Shooter companion controllers, admitted routines both.
`replace_devil_shooter_companion_active_controller` declared the two bytes that
`JSR` pushes at master-cycle offset 6, and the emulator writes them at offset 0.
354 calls a route, two writes each, 708 lines.

**Offset 6 is the right answer to the wrong question.** On the silicon a `JSR`
spends its third and fourth cycles pushing, which is offsets 6 and 9. This core
does not model it that way: the opcode body runs

```
PUSH(PC >> 8);
PUSH(PC);
PC = RdOp(PC) << 8;
...
ADDCYC(6);
LastCycle();
```

so both bytes are stamped with the timestamp the instruction started at, and
the seven cycles are charged afterwards in one go. A transcript is not a
description of the processor; it is a description of what the emulator would
have done, and where those two differ the emulator wins by definition.

**A write is credited at one end of its instruction or the other, and which
end depends on the opcode.** A store lands on its instruction's *final* cycle
-- that was the 02:5408 finding three slices back, `STA $3E00,X` credited at 48
when it belongs at 51. A push lands on its instruction's *first*. Both mistakes
were three or six cycles, both were invisible to every census, and both were
found the same way.

| | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Stack-page writes matching assembly | 4,204,991 of 4,205,699 | **4,205,699 of 4,205,699** |
| Registry cycles | 692,715,369 | 692,715,369 |
| Admitted routines | 404 | 404 |
| Release tests | 420 | **421** |

**The cycle count could not move and that is the point.** A transcript's
`body_master_cycles` was right the whole time; only the attribution inside it
was wrong. Nothing in the registry summary, the state census, or the routine
replay could see it. `--routine-replay` in particular *verified* this exact
routine at `02:53C8@3` and `02:5441@3` on every Release run: it restores a
savestate and re-runs the frame with the same configuration, so both sides of
its comparison were the same replacement agreeing with itself.

**So the oracle is now a test rather than a habit.**
`dc_rom_registry_stack_page_writes` records the whole 3,600-frame route twice
-- once emulated, once with every admitted routine deployed -- and requires the
two traces over `$2100-21FF` to be byte-identical. It is deliberately not a
pinned hash. The two comments this defect class has already left in
`verify_devil_shooter_companion_dormant_semantic.cmake` both say the same
thing: *this hash agreed with the mistake*. A digest states that the registry
still does what it did; the comparison states that the registry still does what
the original does, which is the property the port claims. It costs 33 seconds
and does not extend the suite's critical path (191.4s before, 191.7s after).

The guard was checked for sensitivity by putting the defect back, rebuilding
and re-running it: it fails, and reports the same two hashes the manual traces
produced. 421/421 Release, 3/3 ROM-free Debug. `windows-debug` was not run.

### Previous: the `SEI` stop, removed from the checkpoint format
Done. The largest single instruction the deployed registry
still emulated was one the format could not describe, and the format was wrong.

**`00:FC81` is one `SEI`, and it was 1,509,498 emulated master cycles.** More
than any other instruction outside the frame-sync wait, and more than any
routine still unported. Two slices had worked around the rule that produced it
-- stop in front of the mask set, register the address after it, let the core
run the one instruction -- and the ranking finally priced the workaround:
1,597,272 cycles across eight sites, **13% of everything the registry still
emulated**.

| | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Registry cycles | 691,189,635 | **692,715,369** |
| Share of the route | 53.48% | **53.60%** |
| Share outside the frame-sync wait | 97.28% | **97.50%** |
| Residue outside the wait | 11,964,270 | 10,438,224 |
| Admitted routines | 404 | 404 |
| Interrupt-boundary decisions | 66,291,003 | 66,291,003 |
| Declined at a horizon | 0 | 0 |
| Abandonments | 0 | 0 |

**+1,525,734 master cycles, and not one line of new transcript.** `00:FC81` and
`00:FD75` are gone from the instruction profile entirely rather than reduced.

**The ambiguity was one field, not one byte.** A checkpoint carried a single
status, and the core took two things from it: the `P` an interrupt taken at
that boundary pushes, and the `IFlagSample` deciding whether it may be taken.
`LastCycle` runs before the opcode's writeback, so an `SEI` samples the window
it is about to close -- an interrupt already pending is still taken there, and
pushes the `P` the `SEI` just wrote. But the checkpoint *already* separates the
sample from the boundary in time: `interrupt_sample_master_cycle_offset` exists
for exactly that reason. It simply did not separate them for the mask.
`patches/0023-huc6280-interrupt-flag-sample.patch` adds
`samples_interrupt_flag_clear`; the core applies the clear mask across
`DcSampleInterrupt` and the retired one immediately after.

Three things kept a core change from being a risky one, and they are the
pattern to copy:

- **Additive, with the old behaviour as the default.** A checkpoint that
  leaves the field zero takes byte-for-byte its previous path, so all 404
  admitted routines were unaffected by construction rather than by testing.
- **Refused rather than trusted.** The host throws on a checkpoint claiming the
  clear sample without setting the mask, so the one way to state it wrongly
  cannot reach the core.
- **Proved where a wrong answer would land.** Both readings of an `SEI`
  boundary differ only in the byte an interrupt pushes, so the oracle is the
  stack page: `--work-ram-write-range 2100-21FF` over the whole route,
  **4,205,705 writes, identical**. The state census cannot see it -- a pushed
  byte is popped long before a frame boundary -- which is exactly why the
  census missed the four-byte fault in the slice before this one.

**A pre-existing defect surfaced and is not mine.** The stack trace differs
from pure assembly in 708 of those 4,205,705 writes: same address, same value,
6 master cycles late, at two `JSR`s in bank `02` (`53C8` and `5441`) that each
sit immediately after a `JSR $C018`. Rebuilding without this slice's producer
reproduces the same 708 differences byte-for-byte, so a deployed replacement
under `01:C018` mis-declares six cycles. The census absorbs it at the
frame-sync wait, which is why nothing has caught it. It is the next thing to
look at.

**The fix removes the obstacle; it does not decide the walk.** Bank `45`'s six
`SEI`s were transcribed too, and then reverted. Removing the stop means the
walk carries on through the mask set and holds `interrupt_window_open` across
it -- correctly, since that boundary is genuinely still open -- which made the
staleness guard and the chunk bound conservative over a much longer span:
`45:4142` fell from 3,544 admitted arrivals of 3,604 to 3,216 and `45:485E`
stopped being entered at all, for a net **+129,942**. The driver epilogue has
no such interaction, because its split at the `SEI` is required for an
unrelated reason -- the `$DA` read needs a snapshot from after the window shut
-- so the transcript ends there whatever the mask set costs. Bank `45` needs
its own measurement pass and a third state in the window model; it is not part
of this slice.

420/420 Release, 3/3 ROM-free Debug. `windows-debug` was not run.

### Previous: finishing bank 45, the music sequencer
Done. Nothing in it needed porting: every instruction had been
written already, and 4.4M master cycles a route were being refused by the
walk's own guards.

**The largest single thing the deployed registry still emulated was code it
already had.** Ranking the residue put bank `45` at 4,430,103 master cycles
across three clusters, and every one of them was the sequencer running
interpreted because a transcript had been declined -- `45:4044` admitted 837 of
7,339 arrivals, `45:4015` 1,933 of 3,599. The routine was admitted, entered,
and simply did not run. **Look at the admitted set's own admission rates before
looking for a new routine to port**; a registry row that reads `837 of 7,339`
is a finished port that is switched off five times in six.

| | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Registry cycles | 687,431,079 | **691,189,635** |
| Share of the route | 53.19% | **53.48%** |
| Share outside the frame-sync wait | 96.76% | **97.28%** |
| Bank 45 native | 41,213,268 | 44,971,824 of 45,805,974 |
| Admitted routines | 399 | 404 |
| Routines entered | 332 | 337 |
| Residue outside the wait | 16,740,903 | 13,144,950 |
| Declined at a horizon | 0 | 0 |
| Abandonments | 0 | 0 |

**+3,758,556 master cycles, and every one of them is bank 45.** No other
routine on the route moved. It is between three and five times each of the last
four slices, and none of it came from writing a transcript.

**Three faults, and the first was a list that had drifted.** A family that
stops in front of an `RTS` at depth zero and executes one deeper keeps two
lists of the same addresses. Seven returns -- `4141`, `4243`, `4270`, `429E`,
`42B2`, `42B9`, `46D6` -- were in the stop list and missing from the execute
list, so a walk that inlined a call ending at any of them fell through to
`default` and gave up the whole transcript. `46D6` and `429E` alone were 9,830
refusals on the census route, six times every other cause in the bank put
together. **An address in one list and not the other is a routine that can be
entered and never left.**

**The second was one `SEI`, and then it was six.** A checkpoint carries a
single status byte and the core takes two different things from it -- the `P`
an interrupt taken at that boundary pushes, and the `IFlagSample` that decides
whether it may be taken there at all -- and a mask *set* wants opposite answers,
because `LastCycle` samples before the flag retires. `docs/` had recorded that
from one instance in the sound driver and it read as being about that instance;
bank `45` had six, all transcribed with the deferred set, all latent for
slices. The remedy is the sound driver's: stop in front of it, register the
address after it. `4154`, `4169`, `47E0`, `485E` and `49E4` are those
addresses.

**Make that stop conditional and it costs almost nothing.** The ambiguity only
exists when the `SEI` has a window to close; reached with `I` already set, the
deferred byte and the true byte are the same byte and the walk transcribes it
normally. `4142` brackets every channel in `PHP`/`SEI`/`PLP`, so most arrivals
are masked -- and `4169` is now the busiest entry in the bank at 11,093
arrivals, all admitted, for exactly that reason. Deleting the masked case
instead of keeping it sent every masked arrival to `default`, which is how this
was got wrong the first time.

**The third was reading the mask once.** The driver-state guard exempts a walk
that ran masked, because the driver cannot have changed its bytes since the
snapshot. It read that from `entry.registers.status`, and the tick is called
from inside the VBlank handler -- so it is entered with `I` set, and bank `45`
does not honour that: `4837`, `4872`, `47EE` and `49F2` each end a critical
section with an unconditional `CLI` rather than restoring the caller's mask. A
body entered masked runs most of itself unmasked, and the guard was exempting
all of it. **The mask a body runs under is not the mask it was entered with**,
and following it instruction by instruction is only tractable because the `SEI`
rule above means nothing inside a transcript can close the window.

**The proof is a two-run diff, and it caught the third fault.** The same route
recorded with the family emulated and replaced gives a byte-identical census, a
byte-identical 5,458,568-write work-RAM trace over the voice records, the
zero-page command pointer, the driver's per-channel state and the stack page,
and a byte-identical 699,251-write bus trace over `$0800`-`$0809` and
`$0C00`-`$0C01`. The intermediate version differed by **four bytes in 5.4
million** -- a `PHA` at `45:4847` pushing `$C9` where assembly pushes `$49` --
and the census matched, and all 699,251 device writes matched. Only the stack
page said so.

**Measure why a walk declines; do not reason about it.** Four hypotheses --
the chunk margin, the interrupt horizon, the driver-state guard, the MPR
mapping -- were each plausible, each cost a build and a 3,600-frame run, and
each was wrong. A twenty-line counter at every `return std::nullopt`, keyed by
entry address and stopping program counter, named the real cause in one run and
the second one in the run after that. Nought for four is the record that
matters.

### Previous: the actor scan's preamble
Done. It is the simplest block of its size left in the ROM, and the first slice
whose hand-off is a fall-through rather than a call.

**`01:C4DE`-`01:C50E` settles what the actor scan is about to walk.** It decides
this frame's actor enable mask, resets the three cursors the scan allocates its
list entries from, clears the scan index, and falls into the scan itself. The
mask lands in `$2CEE`, and `$2CEE` is a mask rather than an index: 01:D466 loads
it and ANDs it against each actor's `$3B80,X` attribute byte, so a zero there
turns every actor off for the frame. Four gates can produce that zero --
`$2D35`, `$2CC7`, bit 3 of `<$53`, and on one arm a mask staged in `<$B7`
instead. `$2CBA` and `$2CBB` are the two ends of a single 128-entry list at
`$2BBA`, which is why one is cleared and the other set to $7F; `$2CBC` indexes
the separate list at `$2C3A`; `<$4D` is the scan index 01:C510 reads on its
first instruction.

**775,224 master cycles, and the static model predicted 775,224.** Three slices

same proportion as the last two. Price with the model; rank with the profile.

**Its hand-off is a fall-through, and that is the thing worth keeping.** Every
slice before this one ended a walk either at a return or at a call. This one
ends at neither: the last instruction is `STX <$4D`, and the next address is
01:C510, the registered actor scan. The transcript simply stops in front of an
address this port already owns. A crossing has to push a return frame and buys
the 21 cycles of the `JSR` it converts; a fall-through pushes nothing, converts
nothing and costs nothing, and it works for the same reason a crossing does --
the machine is handed a program counter, and whatever owns that address picks
the body up. **Look for the routine that runs immediately before a registered
one.** It is the cheapest kind of adjacency the port has.

**No call of any kind, and no ROM read.** Twenty instructions, twelve work-RAM
addresses, two immediate constants. There is nothing in it that could reach a
device, so the only thing the transcript has to be right about is arithmetic on
flags and the six bytes it writes.

**One arm is handed back and it has never run.** `$2254` was zero on all 3,492
arrivals, so 01:C4ED and 01:C4EF -- which would take the mask in `<$B7` -- have
not executed once in 3,600 frames. The two branches to 01:C4FC are transcribed
instead, and the distinction is worth keeping: neither of those has been taken
either, but 01:C4FC is live, reached 322 times by the fall-through from 01:C4FA,
so following a branch there lands on an instruction the walk already owns.
**Hand back an arm when its target is outside the transcript, not merely because
the branch has never gone that way.**

**The range has no residue.** All eighteen interior addresses are gone from the
deployed profile; 01:C4DE remains as the registry's own row and 01:C510 as the
next routine's. The same measurement re-run over the seven other ranked

and not in the way it was counted.

**`entries: 3492 of 3492` is again the shared-state argument.** A transcript is
computed from a snapshot, so its reads must all fall inside one interrupt

**The call bucket did not move at all**, which is the arithmetic check on the

### Previous: the shared motion step
Done. It was the most widely shared routine ported so far, and the first family
whose calls went to leaves it owned itself.

**`00:F08E`-`00:F1B3` moves one actor and reports whether it left the
playfield.** `$3800,X` is the actor's motion-enable byte and the head is a
four-way dispatcher on its bottom four bits: bit 0 integrates the vertical
position at `00:F0C0`, bit 1 the horizontal at `00:F104`, bit 2 steps the
vertical velocity toward its target at `00:F148`, bit 3 the horizontal at
`00:F17E`. Position is a twenty-four-bit fixed-point triple and velocity a
signed sixteen-bit pair; the integrators add one into the other with the sign
extended through `$2B`, then stage the whole-pixel word and a bound into
`$2D`-`$30` and call the registered comparison at `00:E93C` -- $0140 across,
$02D0 down, the playfield's two dimensions. Out of bounds bumps `$26`, and the
head turns `$26` into the carry it returns.

**`01:C721`-`01:C770` spends the substeps `01:DC95` splits out.** `$57` is the

its own anywhere and absorbs nothing.

worth taking and what makes it unusual: eight of its thirty-one instructions are

makes it the arm that would catch a transcript whose own artifacts were exact
and which still shifted the machine's event phase around them.

**Shared state was measured rather than assumed.** A pure-assembly write trace
of every write to `$56`, `$57`, `$59` and `$3C80-$3CFF` across the whole route
names every writer: `$57` only `01:DC95`'s five stores; `$56` and `$59` only
this loop, the near-identical pre-loop at `01:C6C9` and the startup `TII`; and
`$3C80,X` bank `01`, `02`, `03` and `08` game code plus `00:F1D7` and `00:F23D`,
which are inside two of the callees. Nothing in the VDC handler, the timer
driver or the music sequencer writes any of it. Those two callee writers are
also why `01:C742` and `01:C74C` are separate entries rather than one long walk:
each re-reads `$3C80,X` after a call that may have written it, and a transcript
stages work RAM once at its entry.

**`Instructions interpreted` did not move again, at 66,291,003.** Same reason as
last slice: it counts interrupt-decision points, not interpreted work, and one
checkpoint per instruction preserves every one of them.

**The registry generator reads the dispatch chain, so write the keys out.** The
first attempt registered the eleven entries through a `switch` predicate;
`Generate-NativeRegistry.ps1 -Check` rejected every one of them as unreachable,
because it matches a literal `entry.routine == RoutineKey{…}` in
`native_replacements.cpp` and nothing else. Matching the pattern it looks for is
the fix, not teaching it a second one -- the check is what stops a routine being
admitted to the registry that the dispatcher would never hand a replacement for.

### Previous: the ball's substep split
Done, and the residue it removed was the whole routine rather than a return.

**`01:DC95` decides how finely one frame of motion is integrated.** It takes
the larger of the two integer motion magnitudes, selects one, two or four
substeps from it, and arithmetic-shifts both signed 8.8 components down to
match, so a fast ball is stepped through the playfield rather than across it.
`01:C721` is the loop that consumes it: `$56` counts substeps, `$57` is the
count this routine wrote, `$59` caps the loop at sixteen, and `01:C770` tail-
jumps back into `01:DC95` to arm the next frame.

**It was the largest self-contained routine left in bank `01` and the only
member of its own neighbourhood nobody had ported.** `01:DD09` sits directly
after it with 4,313,058 native cycles and `01:DD6E` after that; `01:DC95` ran
2,895 times per route with every instruction emulated, 1,002,069 master cycles
across forty-eight addresses. Those forty-eight are now zero.

| | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Registry cycles | 683,629,137 | **684,622,662** |
| Share of the route | 52.90% | **52.97%** |
| Share outside the frame-sync wait | 96.22% | **96.36%** |
| Native calls | 2,686,166 of 2,724,724 | 2,689,061 of 2,727,619 |
| Admitted routines | 375 | 376 |
| Residue outside the wait | 20,570,661 | 19,568,592 |
| Declined at a horizon | 0 | 0 |
| Abandonments | 0 | 0 |

**Nothing about it is a stored expectation.** The proof is the in-run
comparison: the same route traced with the routine emulated and with it
replaced gives byte-identical census, call trace and write trace -- 2,895
calls and 31,737 writes either way, with the call trace carrying each call's
body cycle count, so the cycle model is checked exactly rather than plausibly.

**It is a ninth shape for `verify_absorbed_return_trace`, and a new one: a
routine that is mostly not called at all.** One site reaches it with
`JSR $DC95` and seven with `JMP $DC95`, and 2,340 of its 2,895 arrivals come
through the `JMP` at `01:C770`. On those the frame its `RTS` reads was pushed
by whoever called its *caller*, so the absorbed return skips a level of the
stack that no other absorption in the registry does. The pointer arithmetic is
the ordinary $2100+S+1 and +2, which is exactly why it is worth a test: a tail
call leaves the stack looking normal, so reading it wrong would return to a
live address and keep running rather than fault.

**`Instructions interpreted` did not move, and that is the correct result.**
It counts the points at which the machine decided the next thing to happen was
an instruction rather than an interrupt, not interpreted work. The transcript
carries one checkpoint per instruction, so every one of those decision points
survives the port -- the same reason absorbing the sound driver's `RTI` left
the figure where it was.

**One thing the profile will not tell you, recorded because it cost time.**
The rows over-report slightly: `01:DC95`'s residue profiles at 1,002,069 but
the registry gains 993,525, a 0.85% gap that appears on every row and is the
cycles of interrupts landing inside the instruction being attributed to it.
The static instruction model is the exact one; the profile is for ranking.

### Previous: where the abandoned transcripts go
Done, and it answered a question that was recorded here as the next slice's
first step. It also found something bigger than the slice, which is parked
below rather than landed.

**Nothing about the emulation changed.** `patches/0021` adds three facts to
what the core says and none to what it does; the route is
688,632,969 / 53.28% / 96.92% and 21,657 abandonments exactly as before, and
415/415 Release and 3/3 ROM-free Debug pass.

**`--abandonment-census` names all 21,657 across 904 sites.** The core counts
abandonments whether or not anyone is listening, so the census summing to that
counter is the check that none is missed. The transcript names itself: rather
than keep a map of open transcripts -- impossible, because completion reaches
no hook and completion is the common ending -- the token the host mints carries
the routine key in its low twenty-four bits and the core hands it straight
back.

| Transcript | Abandonments | Distinct resume addresses |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `02:58C2` | 5,034 | 92 |
| `03:7F57` | 4,515 | 95 |
| `01:C510` | 2,637 | 11 |
| `01:C606` | 2,464 | 28 |
| `03:6966` | 1,721 | 71 |
| `01:C52C` | 1,230 | 4 |
| `01:C523` | 813 | 3 |

**The recorded guess about the bank `03` residue was wrong, and the census is
what corrects it.** `PROGRESS.md` had this slice down as the first step toward
`03:6900`-`03:6A80`'s 2,433,327 emulated cycles, on the assumption that they
belong to `03:6966`. They mostly do not. `03:6966` abandons 1,721 times; its
*callers* abandon while running its body, because both of them compose it --
`02:58C2` resumes at `03:699C`, `03:69C7`, `03:6A16`, `03:6A33` and eighty-odd
other addresses inside it, and `03:7F57` resumes at `03:6966`, `03:6982` and
`03:696B`. 11,037 of the route's abandonments resume in bank `03` and only
1,721 of them are the interpreter's own. An address list of interior resume
points was never the answer; there are hundreds and they belong to three
different transcripts.

**All 21,657 are `registers`.** Not one is a transcript mispricing its own
advance, and not one is a transcript resumed past its last checkpoint. The two
other endings the patch can report were never seen. So no transcript on this
route is internally wrong -- every abandonment is the machine coming back from
an interrupt in a state the transcript did not declare.

**All 21,657 of those are `P`, and all 21,657 of those are the B flag.** Never
`A`, never `X`, never `Y`, never an `MPR`; never any other bit of `P`. Measured
by sending the status XOR through the `detail` byte for one run, which decodes
to `0x10` on every site.

**B is not a register bit on this processor.** `PHP` pushes `P | B_FLAG` and
`PLP` pops the byte back whole, so any `PHP`/`PLP` pair -- `03:697C` and
`03:6982` are one, in the middle of the interpreter -- *sets* it in the live
register. Any interrupt clears it again, because that push forces it off and
`RTI` restores what was pushed. Nothing ever reads it: both pushers force it
themselves in opposite directions, and the only other reader of `P` is
`REDOPIMCACHE`, which caches `I`. So the core has been giving transcripts up
over a bit no execution can depend on, and has been doing it 21,657 times.

**So the comparison stopped**
(`patches/0022-huc6280-break-flag-resume.patch`): B is ignored when a resume
point is checked, and a checkpoint leaves the machine's own B standing rather
than writing the transcript's.

| | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Abandonments | 21,657 | **0** |
| Instructions interpreted | 66,312,647 | 66,291,003 |
| Registry cycles | 688,632,969 | 683,629,137 |
| Share of the route | 53.28% | **52.90%** |
| Share outside the frame-sync wait | 96.92% | **96.22%** |
| Admitted routines | 379 | 375 |
| State census | `9036a9de…` | **byte-identical** |

**The reported cycles fall because they were wrong, not because the port got
worse.** The host credits a native call when it *offers* one. An abandoned
transcript was credited its whole body while the emulator delivered only part
of it -- and then, re-interpreting the rest of that same span, the machine
arrived at registered addresses *inside* it and each of those was credited its
own body on top. `02:58C2` abandons 5,034 times and `02:58DD` loses 4,628
entries once the abandonments stop; `03:7F57` abandons 4,515 and `03:7FB1`
loses 3,172. Fifty-two routines move and every one moves down. **52.90% is the
first figure this project has had with nothing abandoned and therefore nothing
counted twice**, and the emulator interprets 21,644 fewer instructions than it
did at 53.28%.

**Four routines lost their last caller.** `02:5893`, `02:58DD`, `03:742B` and
`45:48B4` were reached *only* when the core gave a transcript up and resumed
the composed body in assembly. They were registered because that resumption
was a real arrival; it is not one any more, and the registry is 375 rather than
379. Their replacements are still dispatched and still correct. Four entry
points that existed to catch the fallout of a spurious comparison is a fair
summary of what the comparison cost.

**The host stopped recording B as well, and had to.** A transcript models
`PHP`/`PLP` exactly, so it carries B forward; it cannot know when an interrupt
will clear it. Abandonment used to throw those transcripts away before anyone
could compare them, so with them completing, the declared register reached the
call traces and disagreed with the emulated one -- and the eight
`absorbed_return_trace` regressions, which compare an emulated route against a
replaced one *inside the same run*, caught it. `observable_status` drops the
bit on the way out of the machine and on the way into the core, for the same
reason the core stopped comparing it. All eight pass.

**220 stored expectations moved and every one of them is that bit.** Verified
directly rather than assumed: regenerating `knights-v1.csv.trace.csv` either
side of the change gives one differing column across 10,605 rows, `status`,
and one differing value, `10` -> `00`. The rest are `entries: N of M` counts
that fall by exactly the post-abandonment re-entries the census predicts --
`01:C510` from 176,861 to 175,226 against 2,637 abandonments.

| Site | Into | Walk that reaches it | Executions | Master cycles |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: | ---: |

**Crossing costs a transcript exactly what stopping cost it.** The same two
return bytes on the stack page, written at the same offset — `JSR` pushes both
before charging a cycle, so both carry the instruction's start offset, and the
core breaks that tie by instruction so the pair lands with the call — and the
same twenty-one cycles. What it buys is that the walk ends *on* the callee's
first instruction rather than in front of the call, so the core enters a
registered routine instead of interpreting its way into one.

**`00:E114` is an entry that exists only to cross a call, and it is the half of
this slice worth remembering.** Crossing `00:E111` alone would have bought
57,708 and then handed the machine straight back: `00:EB30`'s return lands on
`00:E114`, and with no hook there the core interprets `JSR $E195` exactly as it
always did. One instruction, registered, whose entire body is a call, is worth
the whole 75,579 the call is worth — more than three of the eleven rows in this
family that do real work. **A one-instruction entry is not too small to be
worth registering; it is worth whatever the instruction is worth.**

**The evidence is that nothing changed.** All three of
`verify_vblank_handler_semantic`'s expected hashes are the ones the file already
carried before any of this existed — census `9036a9de…`, 5,061,032 work-RAM
writes over the whole stack page at `3fb9b061`-era scope hashing
`69dc2054…`, and 2,079,422 bus writes over the VDC's three base ports and the
joypad latch hashing `adc3b5cc…`. Not re-recorded: unchanged. A crossing that
priced the call wrong, pushed the wrong bytes, or wrote them at the wrong offset
would move every push made afterwards, and the whole stack page is in scope. An
unchanged write trace is the strongest thing this test can say about a call: the
transcript does the pushing now and it is indistinguishable from when the core
did.

| Entry | Instructions | Ends on | Native calls | Master cycles |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: | ---: |

exists to switch banks: `TAM #$10` and `TAM #$20` are the point of it, and both
of its halves at `00:E20D` and `00:E200` have been native since the call-wrapper
slice. Bringing eleven instructions in line would transcribe a routine that is
already transcribed and take its MPR changes onto this walk's own register file
for nothing. Push the return, charge 21, end on the callee's first instruction.

**The cycle model was closed before any code was written.** 57 master cycles for
the head and 2,190 for the body — the copy loop is 48 per iteration plus 12 for
each of 31 taken branches and 6 for the last — is 2,247 a call, and 2,247 × 177
is 397,719, which is exactly what the profile attributes to the routine's
fifteen addresses. No interrupt lands anywhere in it on this route, which is
visible in the same place: every row is an exact multiple of its own instruction
cost, with no dispatch charged to any of them.

**The evidence is a comparison, not a recorded expectation.** The same route
traced with the whole stack page, the pointer the walk builds at `$202E`-`$2030`,
the *whole* shadow buffer and all thirty-two dirty flags in scope produces
5,763,953 writes, byte-identical with the family emulated and with both entries
replaced — `3fb9b061…` either way, census the assembly-only `9036a9de…` either
way. The scope is the whole buffer rather than block zero on purpose: a walk
that staged the wrong block, or more than one, would show, and the family's
other producers stay emulated in that run and have to interleave with this one
exactly as they did.

**The second entry is a resumption point, and its return closes someone else's
call.** `08:5982` is where the resolver lands, so it is entered on a frame it
did not push, and the `RTS` it ends past closes the call `08:5977` was entered
on. It is watched at `08:5977` — the shape `00:ECE2` established and `03:601E`
repeated, but this is the first one where the two transcripts are separated by a
call into another bank. Registered as the eighth case of
`dc_rom_absorbed_return_trace`: 177 calls and 9,204 writes, identical either
way.

**The counters.** 376 routines, 309 entered, 2,692,840 of 2,731,425 calls — the
354 added are 177 × 2, all admitted. Nesting, instructions interpreted and
abandonments are all unchanged at 301,698, 66,312,646 and 21,656, which is what
a routine no interrupt ever lands in looks like.

**One incidental fix.** `tests/verify_absorbed_return_trace.cmake` said "Six are
registered" when there were seven, and `tools/Generate-NativeRegistry.ps1`
still carried a stray `**` from the wrapper slice's de-bolding. Both corrected.

### Previous: the Tower-insect controller

Done. The same move again, made against a parent whose children were already
native — which is the case where crossing and composition look most alike.

**`03:6016` was the largest emulated body left on the route.** Six
instructions: load the collision selector from `$3780,X`, `JSR $6966` into the
collision-table interpreter, `BSR $6054` into the animation leaf, load
`$3800,X`, branch on bit 7, `RTS`. Both callees have been registered since this
family was ported and the parent never was, so 6,494 dispatches ran a load, two
calls, a load, a branch and a return through the interpreter to reach code that
was already transcribed. The registry goes 686,981,976 -> **687,682,992**,
53.16% -> **53.21%** of the route and 96.69% -> **96.79%** of it outside the
frame-sync wait.

| Entry | Instructions | Ends on | Native calls | Master cycles |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| `03:6016` | the load, then the `JSR $6966` | `03:6966` | 6,494 of 6,494 | 233,784 |
| `03:601C` | the `BSR $6054` | `03:6054` | 6,494 of 6,494 | 155,856 |
| `03:601E` | the load, the branch, the `RTS` | the caller | 6,487 of 6,494 | 311,376 |

**Composition is written for this shape and is still the wrong answer.** A
parent with native children is exactly what composition exists for, so the
choice had to be made on something other than the call count. The test that
decides it is what the parent reads *after* the call. This one reads nothing:
it passes the selector in the accumulator and takes nothing back, and both
callees are entered at their own addresses either way — so a composed walk
would carry the interpreter's variable-length body and the leaf's 147 or 183
cycles for no cycles at all, and be suspended across more timer interrupts for
it. Crossing both calls instead decomposes the routine into one transcript per
straight-line run.

**The prices came from the opcode table, not from the profile.** `BSR` is case
`$44` — PUSH, PUSH, `ADDCYC(4)`, then the taken branch's `ADDCYC(3)` — so 8 CPU
cycles, 24 master, against a `JSR`'s 21, and it pushes the same two bytes in
the same order before charging anything, so the offset tie is the same one.
Reading the profile confirmed the model rather than supplying it: every one of
the six rows exceeded its instruction cost by an exact multiple of 24 master
cycles, which is the interrupt entry sequence charged to the last address
sampled. 271 of those across the six, and they are dispatch, not the routine.

**The seven hits decline.** Bit 7 set means a contact, and everything past the
branch — the 10-unit award, audio command `$29`, the two-hit counter, the slot
release, the tail-call into the generic slot clear — is the rule itself and
stays with the assembly. So `03:601E` covers 6,487 of 6,494, and the two paths
interleave on the same route.

**The evidence is a comparison, not a recorded expectation.** The same route
traced with the whole stack page, the hit flags, the two-hit counters and the
live-instance counter in scope produces 4,282,022 writes, byte-identical with
the family emulated and with all four routines replaced — so every pushed
return address matches in value, address, order and master-cycle offset, and
the census is the assembly-only `9036a9de…` either way. The routine-call trace
matches too, 6,494 calls and 114,100 writes, `cb5d44ef…` and `7d2174b6…`, which
are the hashes `tools/Analyze-TwoHitTargetSemantics.ps1` has asserted since the
family was mapped. That is the check on the absorbed return at `$603E`:
deleting the boundary the observer completes a call on is the one thing here a
write trace could not have seen.

**Two entries are resumption points rather than call targets.** `03:601C` and
`03:601E` are where a callee's `RTS` lands, so the last walk is entered on a
frame it did not push and returns above where it started. Its absorbed return
is therefore watched at `03:6016` — the head that opened the call — which is
the same shape as `00:ECE2` watched at `00:ECC6`, and it is registered as the
seventh case of `dc_rom_absorbed_return_trace`. It is also the only one of the
seven whose replacement declines on some calls.

**The arithmetic closes and the counters say what changed.** 6,494 × 36 +
6,494 × 24 + 6,487 × 48 = 701,016, which is the measured gain exactly. 374
routines, 307 entered, 2,692,486 of 2,731,071 calls — the 19,482 entered are
6,494 × 3 and the seven declines are the hits. Nesting rose 301,484 ->
301,698. Instructions interpreted rose by 107, to 66,312,646, and abandonments
by the same 107, to 21,656; the gain is the full gross even so.

**One incidental fix.** The dispatch chain in `native_replacements.cpp` hit
MSVC's C1061 block-nesting limit at the three new `else if` clauses. The file
already keeps a flat early-return section ahead of the chain for the same
reason, so the three joined it there rather than the chain being restructured.

### Previous: the bank-call wrappers' four calls

Done. The same move as the sprite emitter's slice, made where the module had
written the refusal down.

**`00:E252`, `00:E26E`, `00:ECDF` and `00:ECFA` were 30,468 interpreted calls,
639,828 master cycles** — the four calls the game's entire cross-bank linkage
exists to make, in a module whose nine entry points had been native since early
in the port. The registry goes 686,342,148 -> **686,981,976**, 53.11% ->
**53.16%** of the route and 96.60% -> **96.69%** of it outside the frame-sync
wait. 30,468 × 21 closes it exactly.

| Address | The call | Crossings | Master cycles |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| `00:E26E` | `JMP [$2CBE]`, into the callee's `$40xx` | 11,671 | 245,091 |
| `00:E252` | `JSR $E262`, into the trampoline | 11,599 | 243,579 |
| `00:ECDF` | `JSR $ECF2`, into the sequencer's entry | 3,599 | 75,579 |
| `00:ECFA` | `JMP [$2047]`, into bank `$45` at `$4003` | 3,599 | 75,579 |

**The refusal was a cost mistaken for an obstacle.** The module's own header
said the walk stopped in front of both indirect jumps "rather than resolving
them", and gave the reason: each reads a vector the same transcript just wrote,
so leaving them to the core "removes the only place this module would have to
compute a resume bank." That is a sentence about how much work resolving one
is, not about whether it can be done. The target is always `$40xx`, so the bank
is MPR2 — the slot the prologue mapped from `$30` two transcripts earlier and
still carries live in `registers.mpr`. Two lines.

**Both jump shapes cost 21 master cycles.** Mednafen charges `ADDCYC(6)` for
case `$20` and for case `$6C` alike, and each opcode's own fetch is the
seventh, so a `JMP ($nnnn)` is priced exactly like a `JSR` and simply pushes
nothing. The profile confirms it to the cycle for the two in interrupt context:
`00:ECDF` and `00:ECFA` measured 75,579 each, which is 3,599 × 21 with no
remainder. The two on the main thread measured 1,872 and 1,968 above their
crossing cost, which is interrupt dispatch charged to the last address sampled
— those cycles are dispatch and stay where they are.

**Resolving a vector moves where it is read, and that needed an argument.** The
machine reads `$2CBE` at the jump; the transcript reads it when the walk is
built, five instructions earlier instead of three. Nothing can use that window
which could not already break the game, because a wrapper jumps through a cell
it has just written — anything able to overwrite it in between would send the
assembly itself to a wrong address. A write trace scoped to both vectors names
every writer and finds no preemption: `$2CBE`/`$2CBF` is written by
`00:E264`/`E269` and by `02:4101`/`4107`, `$2047`/`$2048` by `00:ECF4`/`ECF8`
and by the palette upload at `00:EB57`/`EB89`, each a straight-line writer of
its own vector.

**The regression passed with the hashes it already had, and that is the
verification.** `verify_bank_call_wrappers_semantic` has traced the whole stack
page and both vectors since the family was ported, against a pure-assembly run
of the same route. So when the transcripts took the calls over, the trace had
to keep matching a recording made before this module pushed a byte of its own:
6,389,776 writes, `7beefad7…`, and the census `9036a9de…`, all unchanged. A
pushed byte with the wrong value, the wrong order or the wrong master-cycle
offset breaks a hash that was already there — including the offset tie, since
`JSR` charges no cycle before it pushes and both bytes carry the instruction's
start offset.

**It adds no routine, no entry point and no call.** 371 routines, 304 entered,
2,673,011 of 2,711,589 calls, and all nine wrapper entry counts unchanged.
Nesting rose 301,246 -> 301,484. Instructions interpreted rose by 11, to
66,312,539, and abandonments by the same 11, to 21,549 — eleven boundaries
across 3,600 frames that fell differently because the transcripts around them
are one instruction longer. The gain is the full gross of 639,828 even so, so
whatever those eleven are, they are not cycles.

**A simplification fell out.** With all four calls crossed, every stop this
module has is an `RTS`, so `is_stop_instruction` and `absorbable_return_pops`
had the same domain and the first is gone.

### Previous: the sprite emitter's four calls

Done. The walks make the call instead of stopping in front of it.

**`08:4036`'s four `JSR $40DF` were 73,818 interpreted subroutine calls,
1,550,178 master cycles** — the largest single block of assembly left on the
route once the interrupt returns were taken, and the only item on the previous
ranking that was neither a refusal nor residue. The registry goes 684,791,970
-> **686,342,148** native cycles, 52.99% -> **53.11%** of the route and
96.38% -> **96.60%** of it outside the frame-sync wait. 73,818 × 21 closes it
exactly.

**Nothing was blocking them.** The SAT driver is a shared walk across five
entry points, each ending in front of a `JSR` into the sprite emitter, and the
reason it stopped there was that the callee is 944 cycles and twenty-one calls
a frame — far too much to compose. That is a true statement about the *body*
and it was read as a statement about the *call*. A transcript ends by naming
the next instruction, and nothing requires that instruction to be inside the
routine that produced it. So the walk pushes the return address, charges the
21 cycles, and ends on `08:40DF` — the emitter's own registered entry, which
picks the body up exactly as it did when the core interpreted the `JSR`.

**This is a third option beside composition, and a cheaper one.** Composition
subsumes the callee to absorb the call *and* its `RTS`, and pays for the extra
length in shadowing — the collision sweep's slice gave 19.7% of its gross back
that way. Crossing the call adds one instruction to the transcript and nothing
to its span, so it pays no shadowing bill at all: gross and net are the same
number here. The `RTS` half was already absorbed by the emitter two slices
before this one, so the family now pays neither half of the 42-cycle tax.

**It adds no routine, no entry point and no call.** The registry stays at 371
routines, 304 entered, 2,673,011 of 2,711,589 calls; all five SAT entry counts
and the emitter's 73,818 are unchanged to the call. Only the cycles move, and
only out of the interpreter. Nesting rose 300,708 -> 301,246; abandonments are
unchanged at 21,538; instructions interpreted is 66,312,528 for the fourth
consecutive slice, which is what that figure counting boundary *decisions*
rather than interpreted work looks like — the walk used to end and let the core
decide at the `JSR`, and now it ends and lets the core decide at `08:40DF`.

**The verification is a two-run diff, not a recorded hash.** The SAT
regression's write trace gained the stack page `$2100`-`$21FF`, so every
pushed address, its order and its master-cycle offset are pinned: 4,438,966
writes, byte-identical between the replaced route and the same route with
nothing replaced (`6cbeecb8…`), and the state census unchanged at
`9036a9de…`. That check matters more than usual here, because a wrong pushed
word would not fault — the emitter reads it back through its absorbed `RTS`
and would return to some other real address and keep running.

**Two details make the push exact**, both already in the workflow doc and now
cross-referenced from it. `JSR` pushes before it charges a cycle, so both
bytes carry the instruction's start offset — which is also the preceding
checkpoint's offset, and the core disambiguates a tie by instruction rather
than by offset, so the pair lands with the call and an interrupt at the earlier
boundary finds a stack the call has not touched. And the pushed value is the
`JSR`'s last byte rather than the next instruction, because the emitter's
absorbed return reads that word and adds one.

The walk also states the assumption the family had been leaning on unspoken:
its queue reads, its `PHY`/`PLY` and now its pushes all come out of one
private copy of work RAM, which is only the stack while MPR1 selects `$F8`.
The guard declined nothing.

Done. Two entry points of one instruction each, and the sequel the
previous slice made reachable.

**`00:E135` and `00:E194` are the `RTI`s the VDC interrupt leaves through** —
7,198 of them on the shared epilogue and 387 on the secondary handler's,
**159,285 master cycles**. They were the only interrupt returns left on the

**96.38%** of it outside the frame-sync wait.

**The finding is the shape, not the size.** The walk cannot cross the `PLP` in
front of each return — that is the rule the handler's own slice settled, and it
still holds — so the returns were recorded as unreachable. They are not: what
cannot be crossed can be entered on the far side of. Both are entries of one
instruction, taken after the core has interpreted the `PLP` between them, and
the replacement hook fires at every instruction boundary so no new capability
was needed to admit an address nothing jumps to. That is worth carrying: an
instruction a transcript cannot express blocks the walk, not the address past
it.

**It cost one guard and one line of resume handling.** The entry states the
assumption the whole family had leaned on silently since it was written — that
MPR1 selects work RAM, which is what makes the walk's private copy the stack —
and declines rather than guesses. It declined nothing; all nine existing
entries hold their counts exactly. And like the driver's return, the resume
lands wherever the machine was when the interrupt was taken, so its bank is
resolved through the MPRs the transcript publishes rather than assumed to be
bank `00`.

**The evidence is the regression that already existed, unchanged in scope.**
`dc_rom_vblank_handler_semantic` censuses the whole stack page at
`$2100`-`$21FF` alongside the VDC and joypad ports, which is exactly what a

and native cycles by 159,285, which is `7,585 × 21` to the cycle.
"Instructions interpreted" is 66,312,528 either way for the third slice
running, which is the same corrected reading of that figure as before.

**One instrument note this slice adds.** Absorbing the driver's `RTI` deleted
its profile row; making these two entries left their rows exactly where they
were — same executions, same cycles, only the entry-point flag changed. Both
are consistent with the instruction no longer being executed, so a profile row
is not evidence either way and the census is what settles it.

**The stale figures I could check, I fixed.** `NATIVE_REGISTRY.md` calls itself
generated, and its header said 366 routines and 3,452,755 calls against a real
371 and 3,509,295; its VDC table was missing the two dispatcher halves and

### Previous: the sound driver's interrupt return

One instruction, and the largest one still emulated anywhere on the route
outside the frame-sync wait.

**It was the biggest thing left and it was on the deliberate-refusal list.**
`00:FC8D` and `00:FD81` are the `RTI`s the two epilogues end on. They ran
251,852 and 2,751 times for **5,346,663 master cycles** — 17% of everything
still emulated outside the frame-sync wait, and nine times the largest slice
before it. This file and `NATIVE_REGISTRY.md` both listed them as left on
purpose, on the grounds that "returning from an interrupt is the frame
boundary's work, not a transcript's". That was an assertion rather than a
measurement, and it was wrong. The registry goes 679,286,022 -> 684,632,685
native cycles, **52.97%** of the route and **96.36%** of it outside the wait,
and neither address executes again.

**It is expressible for the reason an absorbed `RTS` is**, and it differs in
two ways worth stating: three bytes off the stack rather than two, and it lands
on the address it read rather than one past it, because `JSR` stores the
address of its own last byte where the interrupt sequence stores the one it was
about to run.

**What made it safe to publish is the `SEI` question asked again with the
opposite answer.** A checkpoint carries one status byte and the core takes two
things from it: the `P` an interrupt taken there would push, and the
`IFlagSample` deciding whether one may be taken there at all. The `SEI` ten
bytes earlier is emulated because those disagree. For `RTI` they cannot —
Beetle restores `P` before `LastCycle()`, so the flag the return produced is
the one the boundary is judged on. What separates the two is not the opcode but
where inside the instruction the mask is sampled, which is a thing to check
before assuming the next interrupt-shaped instruction is out of reach.

**The resume needed one thing no other transcript has needed.** Every other one
ends inside the routine that owns it; this one lands wherever the machine was
when the timer took it, which is a different bank on most arrivals. The
declared resume now resolves its bank through the MPRs the transcript is
publishing rather than assuming bank `00`. The walk also states the assumption
it had leaned on silently since it was written — that MPR1 selects work RAM, so
its private copy is the stack — and declines instead of guessing. It declined
nothing: 254,990, 251,531 and 2,758 entries, unchanged.

**Two counters that did not move carry as much as the one that did.** Nesting
stayed at 297,776 transcripts, 3 deep, none refused, so returning straight into
a suspended transcript resumes it exactly as the emulated `RTI` did. And the
instruction-boundary model reports 66,312,528 decisions either way, to the
decision — the machine judged its interrupts at precisely the same points.
That last one also corrects a comment in `main.cpp`: the figure it prints is
not "instructions the host interpreted", because applying a checkpoint returns
to the top of the same loop and asks the same question, so 254,603 `RTI`s
stopped being interpreted without moving it at all.

**Found on the way, and not fixed here: `docs/NATIVE_REGISTRY.md` says "do not
edit by hand" and is no longer what its generator produces.** Running
`tools/Generate-NativeRegistry.ps1` over the committed tree — before any edit of
this slice — rewrites the document with 416 lines deleted and 56 added, and the
deleted ones are prose that exists only in the document. So regenerating is
currently destructive, and the banner is advice nobody has been able to take;
the header counts alone are three routines and fifty thousand calls stale. The
`dc_native_registry_manifest` regression does not catch it, because what it
compares is `native_registry_table.inc`, which regenerates identically. This
slice edited both files to say the same thing and left the drift alone — it is
a few hundred lines of reconciliation and belongs to a slice of its own, before
someone runs the generator and loses the difference.
