### Previous: the per-run test failure, deferred for four slices

It is not a port slice at all: nothing in the registry
moved, no artifact changed, and the deliverable is that the validation gate
every other slice is measured against stops lying about once per run.

**It was never a divergence.** Every captured instance carries one message —
`Could not commit <artifact>; Windows error 32` — raised after the route had
run and every replacement had reported its entry count. The recorders write
`<path>.tmp` and end with `MoveFileEx(..., REPLACE_EXISTING)`, and that replace
is the one step another process can refuse. Four instances now exist across four
unrelated regressions: `dc_rom_palette_shadow_semantic` and
`dc_rom_actor_camera_sweep_semantic` at `-j 6`, the work-RAM and census
artifacts respectively, plus
`dc_rom_knight_terminal_release_helper_post_return_position_high_scratch_add_prefix`
captured deliberately this slice at `-j 24`. Four different tests with one
message is a property of the commit, not of any of them.

**The dates settle it independently of the message.** `-j 24` arrived in
`074fb10`; there have been exactly eight slices since, and the failure was seen
about once per run across those eight. Serially, over hundreds of runs, it never
appeared. Nothing about the emulation changed at `074fb10` — only how many of
these processes close a large file at the same moment.

**Which of the two files the scanner holds was measured, and the intuitive
answer is wrong.** A handle on the destination is refused with
ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED; only a handle on the temporary gives error 32. Every
message from the suite was error 32, so what was held was the artifact the
process had just written and closed -- which is what an on-close scan is for --
not the older file being replaced. This was not reasoned out: the first version
of the regression modelled a held *destination*, failed, and the failure is what
produced the distinction.

`devils_crush::core::commit_replacement` now performs the replace and retries
while the refusal is one another process can stop causing --
ERROR_SHARING_VIOLATION, ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED, ERROR_LOCK_VIOLATION,
ERROR_USER_MAPPED_FILE -- on a doubling backoff inside a five-second budget.
Every other error still fails on the first attempt, and so does a transient that
outlasts the budget, so a genuinely denied destination fails inside the same run
instead of hanging it. All fifteen commit sites go through it: thirteen in
`main.cpp`, the cabinet configuration and the backup RAM.

**The end-to-end proof is on the shipped binary, not only on the helper.**
Holding a recorder's temporary open for three seconds -- sharing read and write
but not delete, so the recorder keeps writing and only the rename is refused --
produced

```
Committed Canonical recording after 27 retries; Windows error 32.
Canonical recording complete: 600 frames
```

and the committed file is byte-identical to the suite's own canonical artifact,
`67a55bed2d4f4e8dc5019c2b9b845df2f29514bbb564e2e44cde406d159575fe`, with no
temporary left behind. Before this slice that run exits 1.

**One regression was found on the way and closed.** The high-score autosave
commits from inside the frame loop, where five seconds of waiting out a scanner
would be a visible stall rather than a saved write. That caller does not face
the loss the budget exists to prevent -- a failed store stays pending, the poll
returns twice a second, and the flush at shutdown gets the last word -- so it
keeps a single attempt and shutdown keeps the full budget.
`backup::save_atomic` takes the budget for that reason.

**Do not expect to see an absorbed wait in a green suite log, and do not read
its absence as the race having stopped.** Each verify script captures the
recorder's stdout into an `execute_process` `OUTPUT_VARIABLE`, which CTest
surfaces only on failure, so the retry line is swallowed by the same capture
that would have shown the failure. The outcome evidence is five clean full
Release runs after the fix -- 2,055 test executions, 0 commit failures, against
roughly one per run before. The mechanism evidence is `test_atomic_commit`,
which is deterministic: it takes the same no-sharing handle a scanner takes,
releases it part way through the wait, and pins both error codes, the
zero-budget refusal that reproduces the old behavior, the expired budget, and a
missing source failing at once rather than waiting.

411/411 Release, six runs. 3/3 ROM-free Debug in both configurations. The
`windows-debug` sweep was not run.

### Previous: the fork patch `01:C510` was waiting on

It is the first slice in this run that changed the emulator rather
than the port, and the only one whose deliverable is a *report* rather than a
replacement.

`01:C510`, the actor scan loop, now absorbs its return: `01:C52B` falls 73,536
-> 819 master cycles, bank `01` 187,590 -> 114,873, and the route 1,635,210 ->
1,562,493. The registry goes 679,191,291 -> 679,286,022 native cycles, **52.56%**
of the route and **95.61%** of it outside the frame-sync wait. Nested installs
297,770 -> 297,776, three deep at the most, nothing refused, 0 declined at an
interrupt horizon, and the census is `9036a9de...` unchanged.

**The patch is 130 lines and says one thing: the core gave up on a
transcript.** A checkpointed transcript is abandoned when the machine does not
come back to a resume point in the state the transcript declared -- an
interrupt handler that returns a register changed, or that leaves through a
different path. The core has always handled that correctly by interpreting the
rest of the routine, which is exactly why nothing needed telling for as long as
a transcript only *replaced* work. Absorbing a return is a transcript that also
*declares* work, and an undelivered declaration has to be withdrawn.

`patches/0020-huc6280-replacement-abandonment.patch` gives
`PopReplacementFrame` a `completed` argument, so the single place that ends a
transcript is the single place that decides which ending it was: reaching the
last checkpoint while still live is completion and every other way out is not.
The transcript is named by the host -- a `transcript_token` the core stores,
carries across suspensions and hands back, and never reads. The runtime erases
the pendings that token names. A savestate load forgets every token it
restored, because those name some other host's transcripts.

**The evidence is four runs of the same comparison, and it is worth keeping.**
`01:C510` swallows its own loop, so it is joined on entry cycle rather than
compared file to file -- 446,976 emulated calls, 176,861 replaced, every
replaced call present in the emulated set on all four:

| Build | Rows differing |
| --- | --- |
| Absorption on, no patch | `output_y` 82,201, `output_status` 83,084, `MPR4`/`MPR5` 42,753 |
| Withdrawing on the core's own `RTS` | `output_y` 129,236, `output_status` 83,571, `MPR4`/`MPR5` 46,862 |
| Absorption backed out | none |
| **Absorption on, with the patch** | **none** |

The third row is the control the last slice shipped; the fourth is this one.
The half-fix in the second row made it worse, which is the thing to remember
about it -- it was not a partial improvement, it was a different wrong answer.

**The patch does not unblock bank `03`, and the note that said it might was
wrong.** `03:6A37` + `03:6988` are 176,025 cycles of residue on a routine that
*already* absorbs at its entry wrapper: transcripts an interrupt cut short, and
arrivals through the three composition sites that call the interpreter
directly. Both are cycles the assembly genuinely runs, so no report about them
recovers anything. Their rows are unmoved at 154,521 and 21,504 after this
slice, which is how that was settled rather than argued.

**The core now counts what it abandons.** `dc_beetle_replacement_abandonments`
is incremented whether or not a hook is listening and whether or not the
transcript was named, so it measures the core rather than the host's
bookkeeping, and `--replace-registry` prints it. The census route abandons
21,538 transcripts. Nothing consumed that number before this slice and nothing
depends on it now; it exists so that the next family held back on this can be
told apart from one that simply never ends where it says it will.

Two full Release runs, 181 s each, and each had exactly one failure: first
`dc_rom_vblank_handler_semantic`, then `dc_rom_bank_call_wrappers_semantic`.
Both passed alone in under 18 s, both are families never seen to flake before,
and that makes eight distinct families now. **The pattern is stable enough to
stop calling it a flake and start calling it a defect in the harness**: a
different test every time, never reproducible alone, roughly one per full run.
It has been deferred for four slices and should be the next thing after this or
the one after. 3/3 ROM-free Debug. The `windows-debug` sweep was not run.
(It was the next thing: see the current slice. The call above was right that it
is a defect in the harness and wrong about where -- it is not CTest, it is the
artifact commit being refused by a scanner.)

The patch was checked against a tree carrying `0001`-`0019` and none of this
slice's edits, and both halves of the CMake path were exercised: applying it to
that tree, and the already-applied marker branch on the tree it was written
against.

**No pop counts, and it is worth saying why not.** Bank `00` needed them
because its wrappers are written in two halves and the second half returns
above where it was entered. Nothing here does: this bank's returns close the
call their own entry opened, so the test is the plain one -- the pointer still
stands where the entry left it. The bank does contain the other shape, twice.
`45:4579` and `45:4BE6` each push an address and `RTS` to it, which is a jump
rather than a return; both were already absent from the stop list, and the
pointer test would have refused them anyway, standing two below the entry's.

**Three of the fifteen entries do not compare, and the reason is older than
this slice.** `45:4044`, `45:409C` and `45:4143` are loop heads reached by a
`JMP` rather than a call, and replacing a loop head coarsens the call trace:
the iterations the walk runs inside one transcript stop being separate calls.
At `45:4143` the emulated route records 19,062 calls and the replaced one
9,602. Every replaced call is present in the emulated trace verbatim -- 0
absent, 9,460 swallowed -- but a subset is not a match, so I rebuilt with the
absorption removed and traced all three again. The replaced artifacts are
**byte-identical** to the ones the absorption produces, census, call trace and
call-write trace alike. The coarsening is what replacing a loop head has always
done, and the absorbed-return declaration changed nothing about those records.
The other twelve entries compare byte-identically, emulated against replaced.

**What is left in bank `45` is mostly not in the ported set.** Of the remaining
68,481, some 20,000 sits on addresses the walk never stops at -- `45:496C`
(6,387), `45:4559` (3,255), `45:494B` (2,841), `45:4B85` (2,442), `45:495E`
(2,352), `45:4579` (1,701), `45:4CB8` (1,386) -- and the rest is residue on
listed stops, led by `45:46D6` (10,416 of 47,526) and `45:4210` (10,122 of
76,044): transcripts that declined, or that stopped short of the return.

The registry table needed no regeneration -- `Generate-NativeRegistry.ps1
-Check` reports it current at 369 admitted routines, because absorbing a return

### Previous: carrying the absorbed return into bank `00`

Six edits, and it is the slice that found the pointer a return is reached with
need not be the one its routine was entered with.

Bank `00` held 857,328 emulated return cycles, the largest pool left after bank
`01`. It falls to 162,675 -- fourth of eight -- and the route to 2,211,126. The
registry goes 677,903,067 -> 678,599,007 native cycles, **52.51%** of the route
and **95.51%** of it outside the frame-sync wait. Nested installs rose 297,374
-> 297,634, three deep at the most, nothing refused, and 0 calls declined at an
interrupt horizon. The state census is `9036a9de...` unchanged.

**Four of the bank's six families already ended at a fixed set of addresses,
so the edits were cheap.** The bank-call wrappers were the whole of the first one: nine entry
points share `replace_bank_call_wrappers`, five of its nine stops are `RTS` and
all five are returns, each stop is reachable from exactly one entry, and nothing
composes the walk -- so one absorption at the terminus took 475,071 master
cycles. `00:E261` alone is 245,475, the largest row absorbed since `08:41AB`.
The tilemap upload gave three more the same way, the position integration and
the cached-position restore one each, the camera sweep one, and the VBlank
handler's pad reader one.

**A wrapper is written in two halves, and the second half returns above where it
was entered.** `00:E241` saves the two MPR shadows and stops in front of `JSR
$E262`; the core makes the call; control comes back not to `00:E241` but to
`00:E255`, a registered routine in its own right, which pulls the shadows back
off and returns two bytes above its own entry, on the frame `00:E241`'s caller
pushed. `00:ECC6`/`00:ECE2` is the same one shadow wider, three bytes up, and
taken in interrupt context. `absorb_return`'s stack-pointer argument has always
meant the pointer *at the return*; every family before `01:C5C9` merely had the
two equal. So each stop now carries the count of what its walk gave back rather
than being tested for equality with the entry -- 0, 0, 0, +2 and +3 for the
wrappers, and +1 for the tilemap's `00:F43C`, whose `PHY`/`PLY` pair is balanced
across a loop iteration but not across a transcript because `00:F423` sits
between them and is handed to the core.

**A routine of that shape cannot be watched, and that is the instrument rather
than the routine.** The observer opens a call at the entry pointer and closes it
on the next `RTS` standing there; `00:ECE2` has none at that depth, so the call
stays open and collects the rest of the route's writes. The trace passed twenty
gigabytes before I stopped it. The call `00:ECF1` actually closes was opened at
`00:ECC6`, so `verify_absorbed_return_trace.cmake` now takes an `OBSERVE`
argument and the sixth test -- `dc_rom_absorbed_return_trace_handed_over` --
replaces `00:ECE2` while watching `00:ECC6`. It is the only absorbed return
taken in interrupt context.

Twenty-two emulated-versus-replaced comparisons, one routine at a time, all
byte-identical across census, call trace and call-write trace. `00:F523`
(28,813 of 28,823) and `00:F54E` (28,575 of 28,579) report partial admission;
both figures were already in the registry table before this slice.

**What is left in bank `00` is mostly out of reach rather than unported.**
`00:E32B` is 75,123 of the remaining 162,675 and is the frame-sync waiter's own
return: `00:E321` spins on `$00` until the VBlank handler changes it, which no

instructions the spin falls out into -- as an entry of its own, but that is a
new admission with its own regression rather than an absorption, so it is
written down rather than taken. The rest is the unported family around
`00:F0A0`-`00:F1B3` (70,662 across five rows) and small change.

### Previous: carrying the absorbed return into bank `01`

Done, in twenty-one absorptions across fifteen families, and it is the
first slice where a family had to be held back rather than shipped.

Bank `01` held 1,060,104 emulated return cycles, the largest pool left. It falls
to 187,590 -- fifth of eight -- and the route to 2,905,779. The registry goes
677,038,098 -> 677,903,067 native cycles, **52.45%** of the route and **95.41%**
of it outside the frame-sync wait. Nested installs rose 297,017 -> 297,374,
three deep at the most, nothing refused, and 0 calls declined at an interrupt
horizon. The state census is `9036a9de...` unchanged. Twenty-three rows go to
zero.

**A third of the bank came from two edits, because two of its families are
walking interpreters.** `replace_collision_tail` and
`replace_actor_geometry_leaf` each end by stopping in front of whichever address
in a fixed `is_stop_instruction` list the walk reached, and each is dispatched
for many registered entries -- nineteen and two -- so one absorption at the
walk's terminus covers every return the family has: 213,939 master cycles for
the first and 158,472 for the second. Neither routine is composed by anything,
so the return belongs inside the routine and needs no wrapper. That shape is
worth looking for before ranking a bank row by row.

**The stop list had to be read rather than counted.** Eleven of the collision
tail's twenty-five stops are `RTS` and only ten of those are returns.
`01:CBF9` closes the confirmed-contact dispatcher by pushing a vector out of the
tables at `01:CBFA`/`01:CBFF` with two `PHA`s and letting the `RTS` jump to it,
so the word it pops is one the routine wrote two instructions earlier rather
than a frame a caller pushed. `absorb_return` reads the staged transcript rather
than entry work RAM, so it would have computed the right landing address and
still been wrong -- it would have told the observer a call completed where none
did. The stack-pointer test would have caught it as a side effect, the two
pushes having moved the pointer, but that is an accident rather than a reason.

**Three routines needed the entry wrapper, and one of them is a new shape.**
`01:C5C9`, the coroutine scheduler, is run in line by twenty-seven walks in
`native_replacements_rules.cpp`, each of which adopts its `return_instruction`
and `body_master_cycles` as its own and several of which test that the body is
exactly 159 cycles -- so a scheduler that ran past its own return would have
made every one of those compositions fail its guard and fall back silently. It
is also the first absorption whose frame is not where the entry's stack pointer
says: its first two instructions are the `PLA`s that take its own return address
off the stack to record where it was called from, so the `RTS` reads its
caller's caller's frame, at $2100+S+3 and +4 rather than the +1 and +2 every
other absorption reads. Reading the wrong pair there would not look wrong -- it
would return to the
address the routine was called from, which is a real address the machine would
go on executing. That is why it is now the fifth routine in
`dc_rom_absorbed_return_trace`. `01:CC1A` and `01:CC98` are the other two
wrappers, both composed by the sweep at `01:CB48`, which tests which `RTS` the
child stopped on before it will splice it.

**`01:CC98` is correct and idle.** The native cycle census reports 0 entries for
it with the whole registry deployed: the sweep composes the mask lookup on every
call, so nothing arrives at it from the core. Its 18,522 cycles at `01:CCD2` and
`01:CCD4` are the *scan's* transcripts ending in front of the child's return,
which is a different edit and was not attempted.

**One family was held back, and it is the technique's second limit.**
`01:C510`, the actor scan loop, is both long enough to be cut short often and
re-entered at the same stack depth. A transaction stages the return it will
absorb when it is *installed*, and the observer redeems the promise at the
boundary the machine lands on afterwards; nothing withdraws it when the
transcript never gets that far. For every family shipped so far that is
harmless -- the core interprets the rest, executes the `RTS`, closes the call
correctly, and the stale promise is redeemed one boundary later against a call
that is already closed. It stops being harmless when the routine is re-entered
at the same depth, because then the stale promise finds a live victim. Traced
emulated against replaced, `01:C510` reported the wrong `Y` on 82,201 of 176,861
calls and the wrong `MPR4`/`MPR5` on 42,753, with every cycle column still
right -- which is exactly why the comparison catches it and a census hash does
not.

Both halves of the diagnosis were built rather than assumed. The control run
with the absorption removed agreed with the emulated run on every shared column,
which made the difference this slice's. A candidate host fix -- withdrawing the
promise when the core executes the `RTS` itself -- was written, built and
measured: it fixed three calls in eight and no more, because a cut-short scan
usually leaves through the dispatch at `01:C52C` and never reaches `01:C52B` at
all. It was backed out rather than shipped half-working. The real fix is the
core telling the runtime when it abandons a transcript, which is a fork patch
and its own slice. Until then `01:C52B` keeps its 73,536 master cycles and is
the largest single thing left in the bank.

### Previous: carrying the absorbed return into bank `03`'s remainder

Done, in twenty-two edits, and the first two needed a distinction the previous
three slices never had to make.

Bank `03` held 1,498,290 emulated return cycles, the largest pool left. It falls
to 624,837 and the route to 3,778,293. The registry goes 676,133,460 ->
677,038,098 native cycles, **52.39%** of the route and **95.29%** of it outside
the frame-sync wait. Nested installs rose 296,732 -> 297,017, three deep at the
most, nothing refused, and 0 calls declined at an interrupt horizon. The state
census is `9036a9de...` unchanged.

**The two biggest returns belong to routines that cannot absorb them.**
`03:6966`, the collision-table interpreter, is the busiest routine on the route,
and `03:7FB1`, the collision response, sits behind it. Both are *shared*: the
same function answers the registered entry the core takes and the sites that run
it in line -- the Sorcerer tick's two calls, `03:7F57`, `03:73AC` -- and every
one of those reads `return_instruction` to learn which `RTS` the child stopped
on, so that it can transcribe that return into its own transcript at its own
cycle. A routine that ran past its own return would hand all three an address in
the caller and a body twenty-one cycles longer than the one they are splicing,
and they would transcribe the return a second time on top of it.

So the absorption belongs to the *entry*, not to the routine.
`replace_collision_table_entry` and `replace_collision_response_entry` are two
new wrappers that call the shared routine and absorb after it; the registry's
dispatch points at them and nothing else does. The composition sites go on
calling the routines directly and see exactly what they saw before. Each wrapper
still checks what it is absorbing: that the return is one of the routine's own,
that the stack pointer came back to where it started, and -- because the
interpreter's older result-computing path answers atomically on everything its
transcript refuses -- that twenty-one more cycles fit inside the horizon.

| Return | Owner | Master cycles |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| `03:6A37` + `6988` | `03:6966`, collision-table interpreter | 442,578 -> 176,025 |
| `03:7FD1` | `03:7FB1`, collision response | 110,856 -> 21,819 |
| `03:65E9` | `03:65C2`, three-blobs controller | 56,154 -> 0 |
| `03:7B6C` + `7B34` | `03:7B27`, fixed-scheduler gate | 56,154 -> 7,044 |
| `03:6375` | `03:6339`, walled-star hit gate | 56,058 -> 0 |
| `03:74DF` | `03:74D8`, giant-face request gate | 56,040 -> 0 |
| `03:612A` | `03:60C3`, tower hit gate | 55,905 -> 399 |
| `03:7E28` + `7D8A` | `03:7E23`/`7D85`, small-soldier sources | 103,914 -> 0 |
| `03:7748` | `03:7726`, giant-face mouth gate | 25,854 -> 0 |
| `03:66E1` | `03:66DE`, three-blobs continuation | 22,029 -> 147 |
| `03:7BED` | `03:7BEC`, fixed-marker `PLY` tail | 21,036 -> 0 |
| `03:7685` | `03:767E`, giant-face animation gate | 18,549 -> 21 |
| `03:7717` | `03:76FA`, giant-face collision gate | 18,375 -> 0 |
| `03:62D3` | `03:62B8`, giant-door gate | 14,244 -> 0 |
| `03:6401` | `03:63F1`, Devil's-coffin gate | 13,557 -> 0 |
| `03:7E1F` + `7D81` | `03:7E0D`/`7D6F`, delayed spawn | 8,112 -> 1,452 |
| `03:645C` + `6426` | `03:6445`/`640A`, coffin closing and opening | 672 -> 0 |

**Absorbing removes the return only from the calls that finish.** This is the
technique's ceiling and bank `03` is where it became visible. A checkpointed
transcript is replayed checkpoint by checkpoint and can be cut short; when it
is, the rest of the routine is interpreted, including the `RTS` it was going to
absorb. `03:6966` absorbs on every one of its 14,307 registry entries -- native
cycles rise by exactly 14,307 x 21, which is how that is confirmed -- and
`03:6A37` and `03:6988` still execute 8,381 times between them. Eleven of the
twenty ordinary rows went to zero; the ones that did not are the long
transcripts. Nothing in the ranking distinguishes the two beforehand, so the
residue is worth reading after the edit rather than predicting before it.

Two of the twenty-two edits move nothing today. `03:67B3` and `03:67C0` both end
on `03:67E5`, but with the registry deployed they are entered fifteen times each
-- `03:66DE` composes that whole stretch in line -- so the 19,695 cycles at
`03:67E5` are arrivals through paths neither walk owns. The edits are correct
and verified; they are simply not exercised at the top level.

**Proof.** All twenty-two entry points touched here were traced emulated and
replaced, one routine at a time, and the census, the call trace and the
call-write trace are byte-identical across the two runs for every one.
`dc_rom_absorbed_return_trace` now runs over four routines: `03:6966` is the
fourth shape, a return absorbed at the entry rather than inside the routine, and
it is the busiest routine on the route with 54,149 calls when nothing else is
replaced.

valve declines it outright if its body would reach a user event or a
serviceable timer interrupt. Twenty-one more cycles pushed calls over that
line: `02:5397` fell 873 -> 818 admitted, `02:5408` 1,015 -> 952, `02:53DD`
929 -> 832 and `02:5456` 926 -> 830. 311 whole bodies traded for returns, and

room is not there; all four counts returned to what they were, and the route
still declines nothing at a horizon. Eighteen of the twenty-one families are

**The comparison found a defect that predates this slice by four of them.**

**Proof.** Thirty-one of the thirty-two entry points touched here were traced
emulated and replaced, one routine at a time, and all three artifacts are
byte-identical across the two runs for every one of them. Doing it one routine
at a time is not optional: run them together and the comparison is meaningless,
because replaced walks swallow arrivals the emulated observer counts -- the
whole set reports 88,244 calls emulated against 73,187 replaced, which is the
composition working, not a discrepancy. `02:4C78` is the thirty-second and has
nothing to compare: it is entered on this route and admitted on none of those
entries, and once the initializers around it are replaced it is not even
entered.

Done, and it cost two edits.

Bank `08` held 1,726,353 emulated return cycles, the largest pool left, and 95%
of it was two addresses whose walks were already native. It falls to 92,742 and
the route to 5,966,274. The registry goes 673,091,757 -> 674,715,267 native
cycles, **52.21%** of the route and **94.97%** of it outside the frame-sync
wait.

| Return | Owner | Executions | Master cycles |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| `08:41AB` | `08:40DF`, sprite emitter | 73,818 -> 47 | 1,560,450 -> 987 |
| `08:40DE` | `08:40C3`, SAT tail clear | 3,492 -> 0 | 74,148 -> 0 |

`08:41AB` was the largest single emulated instruction anywhere on the route --
more than all eight of bank `03`'s families together. `08:40C3` absorbs on one
arm only: 4,334 arrivals but 3,492 calls, because a run longer than the
transcript's 48-iteration write budget stops at the loop head, which is an
ordinary boundary the next arrival continues from and not a return.

**The bank ranking says nothing about the work.** Bank `03` needed eight edits
for 1,054,221 cycles; bank `08` needed two for 1,633,611. What predicts the
cost is how many of a bank's returns end walks that are already ported, and
everything left in `08` -- `08:5E4C` at 55,845, then `08:5976`, `08:5A69` --
returns from a routine with no transcript. The cheap test is still whether the
address already appears in a walk as a `return_instruction`.

**A second host bug, and the first family that could show it.** The
interrupted-at-the-end recognition used the transcript's own reckoning for the
return's cycle, on the argument that the transcript had run to its end. True,
and not sufficient: that reckoning is fixed when the transaction is installed,
and a transcript long enough to be *suspended* has the whole interrupt handler
inserted into it before it ends. `08:40DF` is both suspended part-way and
interrupted at its end on 58 of its 73,818 calls, and reported those returns
729 cycles early with the last sprite entry's six writes missing. The host now
measures back from the recognising boundary over the return *and* the eight-CPU
-cycle vector sequence, taking the length of a CPU cycle from the gap between
the two bytes of the frame the interrupt just pushed -- consecutive cycles of
that sequence -- rather than assuming the high speed. That needed one new piece
of state: when each byte of the stack page was last written.

This is the same shape as the previous slice's slice-clock bug and the same
lesson twice: **anything a prediction says about when a transcript ended, a
suspension can falsify.** The palette family is never suspended, so no run of
`dc_rom_absorbed_return_trace` could have failed for this. The test now runs
over two routines -- `00:E93C` and `08:40DF` -- registered as two tests so they
run side by side, and the script carries each routine's expected console lines
literally so the registry generator can still read which routines it proves.
`08:40DF` gained a second proof from it.

The regression that found it was the workflow's own rule, followed exactly:
trace the family emulated, trace it replaced, require the census, the call
trace and the call-write trace to be byte-identical. 58 rows of 73,818
differed, all of them calls with an interrupt inside. Then, to be sure the
difference was mine and not pre-existing, the same comparison was run against a
build with the absorption removed: byte-identical to the emulated run, which is
what made it a bug in this slice rather than a discovery about the last one.

`08:40C3` cannot be compared that way -- its transcript swallows the loop the
observer counts, so the emulated run reports 113,810 arrivals against 4,334 --
so the comparison was done as a join on entry cycle instead: all 4,334 replaced
arrivals match their emulated counterpart on return instruction, return cycle,
body cycles, output registers and write count, and the 2,137 of them that write
match write for write.

file says "Do not edit by hand" and the previous slice hand-edited it; a run

671,942,490 -> 673,091,757 native cycles, 52.08% of the route.

| Return | Owner | Executions | Master cycles |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| `03:7F80` | `03:7F57`, no-hit collision consumer | 21,010 -> 4,518 | 441,213 -> 94,878 |
| `03:7387` | `03:7378`, knight release transition | 10,600 -> 0 | 224,712 -> 0 |
| `03:6078` | `03:6054`, tower insect animator | 6,750 -> 355 | 142,950 -> 7,455 |
| `03:65BB` | `03:65A4`, spider appearance | 5,441 -> 90 | 115,557 -> 1,890 |
| `03:78E6` | `03:78C7`, bumper hit gate | 3,457 -> 0 | 73,149 -> 0 |
| `03:7CBB` | `03:7CAF`, fixed response gate | 2,650 -> 0 | 56,298 -> 0 |
| `03:60B2` | `03:60A6`, tower guard selector | 2,650 -> 30 | 56,178 -> 630 |
| `03:7BDF` | `03:7B7A`, fixed scheduler gate | 2,649 -> 332 | 56,157 -> 7,140 |

What is left at each address is the arms the walk does not transcribe -- the
consumer's two-hit path falls through to the same `RTS`, and the classifiers
decline a handful of snapshots -- not returns the technique missed.

**One edit per walk, because the mechanism is now shared.**
`detail::absorb_return` (`native_replacements_absorb.cpp`) takes the state on
the return instruction's own boundary and rewrites the transcript's resume,
output registers, length and final checkpoint from it, pushing the declaration
the observer needs. Every walk above calls it once per arm that reaches a
return. It reads the stack from the *staged* transcript rather than from entry
work RAM: most walks never touch the stack page, but a composition stages its
children's `JSR` frames there, and a walk that stored over its own return
address should fail loudly rather than quietly.

**Which returns are targets is a smaller set than the ranking suggests, and
that is the finding to carry forward.** An emulated `RTS` is only absorbable if
it is the ending of a routine that is *already ported*. Of what remains in bank
`03`, `03:603E` at 137,607 cycles is the second-largest row and is not a target
at all: it is the return of the Tower-insect steady-state parent at `03:6005`,
which composes `03:6966` and `03:6054` and has never been transcribed. Neither
is `03:6533`. Those are blocked on a ported parent, exactly like the `JSR`
half, and a rollout that reads only the ranking will spend its time on them.

**A latent bug in the host, found by the second family and not the first.**
`master_cycle` is a slice timestamp -- it restarts every time the core is
re-entered -- so measuring the deleted boundary by counting back from the
recognition boundary is only right while both are inside one slice. A return
that lands in the last cycles of a slice is recognised at the first boundary of
the next, and the subtraction measures against the wrong origin. `03:7F80` does
this twice on the census route, reporting 9 where the emulated observer
reported 176,064. The slice origin is now recovered from the absolute clock,
which never restarts, and the transcript's own reckoning is used only when the
return is behind that origin entirely. The palette family never straddled a
slice, so the previous slice's regression could not have found this; the
emulated-versus-replaced comparison in this one did, on the first family it was
pointed at.

**And a stale expectation nothing was running.** The one test registered
`CONFIGURATIONS Debug`, `dc_rom_tower_insect_native_family_debug`, compared
against a Debug-only census baseline `a95d0c34...` that the Debug binary no
longer produces. It produces `9036a9de...`, the same as Release. This is not
this slice's doing and cannot be: running the **Debug** binary with no hooks
and no replacements at all -- an assembly-only route no transcript can reach --
produces `9036a9de...`. The two configurations agreeing is the right answer and
the old split was the anomaly, since a build's optimization level has no
business moving a record of machine state. The baseline is corrected and the
test passes in full, including its Debug-specific call and write hashes.

That last point is worth more than the fix. **`03:6054`'s replay still reports
`147 body cycles`** with its return absorbed, and its call and write traces
hash to the values recorded before any of this -- which is the declaration
working under a second observer (`--routine-replay`) and a second build, both
of which this slice's own regression never touches.

### Previous: making the absorbed return visible to the call trace

The slice that had to come before the rollout, and it exists because the
rollout's first step found the slice before *it* had broken an instrument
without any regression saying so.

The plan was bank `03`, the largest remaining pool of emulated returns
(2,552,511 master cycles across 120,611 executions, ranked below). The first
target was `03:7F57`, whose own `RTS` at `03:7F80` is 441,213 of them. Reading
its regression before changing its walk -- the fourth thing the previous slice
said to carry across -- turned up something bigger than the target.

**`--routine-call-trace` completes a call on an emulated `RTS` boundary, and
absorbing the return deletes the boundary it waits for.** It is the observer's
only completion signal: an instruction boundary whose opcode is `$60` at the
stack pointer the call was entered on. With the return absorbed there is no
such boundary, and the observer does not fail -- it waits, and closes the call
on the next ancestor that returns at the same stack pointer.

Measured on the palette family, which the previous slice had already
converted: tracing `00:E93C` reported 8,966 calls instead of 8,969, the first
of them returning to `01:CAB6` after 53,486,487 master cycles instead of to
`00:F0FE` after 78, with 38,057,951 writes recorded against a routine that
makes 12,905. Every artifact the family regression pins -- census, work-RAM
writes, bus writes -- was byte-identical throughout. The machine was right and
the instrument was wrong, and nothing in the suite could tell, because none of
the 315 verify scripts that take a call trace happens to trace a palette
routine.

The control run settles what was at stake. With the replacement deployed but
the absorption disabled, the call trace is byte-identical to the un-replaced
run -- so the instrument had been *exact*, and the previous slice had cost
that without knowing.

**A transcript now declares the return it absorbs**, in
`RoutineReplacement::absorbed_returns`: the return instruction, where its
boundary sits inside the transaction, and the registers at it. The host keeps
the observed call open and closes it when the machine is demonstrably past the
return -- which took two recognitions, not one:

- **The transcript resumed at the caller.** The next boundary stands on the
  resume address with the caller's stack pointer restored. The return's cycle
  is measured *back* from that boundary rather than predicted forward from the
  transaction, which is what makes preemption right: an interrupt taken at a
  checkpoint suspends a transcript rather than cancelling it
  (`PushReplacementFrame`/`PopReplacementFrame`), so the return really happens
  hundreds of cycles after the transaction predicted it.
- **The interrupt took the return.** When delivery lands on the last
  checkpoint the core assigns the resume address and leaves for the vector, so
  the machine never stands on it. Recognised instead from the frame the
  interrupt has just pushed -- three bytes below the returned-to stack pointer,
  carrying the address the return produced -- and there the transcript's own
  reckoning is the right cycle, because it ran to its end.

Each was found by measurement rather than by reading. The first recognition
alone left 54 of 8,969 rows wrong; adding the second left all cycle fields
right and 54 rows carrying three extra writes each, which were the interrupt's
own pushes arriving between the return and its recognition. A call's writes are
now trimmed to those made at or before its return, and the return address comes
from the transaction's resume rather than a second reading of the stack --
because by the time the call is closed, an interrupt may have pushed its own
frame across exactly those two bytes. That last one was a real bug, found the
same way.

**The result is exact.** Three runs of the same route -- routine emulated,
routine replaced without absorption, routine replaced with absorption -- now
produce byte-identical censuses, call traces and call-write traces:
`9036a9de...`, `9818acdf...`, `6f13d0ac...`. The absorbed return is invisible
to the instrument that watches for one.

The regression is `dc_rom_absorbed_return_trace`, and it is deliberately a
comparison rather than a recorded hash: it traces the route with `00:E93C`
emulated and with it replaced and requires all three artifacts to agree. A
recorded expectation could drift into agreeing with a mistake; the emulated run
cannot. It also pins the entry count, because a comparison would pass just as
well if the replacement never ran.

The host validates the declaration: exactly one per transcript, ending that
transcript, leaving `S` two above where the return instruction found it. That
is narrower than what the technique can do, and deliberately so. A return
absorbed on behalf of a *composed* routine part-way through a transcript --
`03:7F57` has absorbed its two children's returns since it was written -- is
not expressible, because the observer cannot recognise by arrival an address
the machine passes through without stopping on. No regression observes a child
while its parent is replaced, so nothing is broken today. It is a known gap,
written down rather than papered over.

### Previous: absorbing the `RTS`

The palette survey below decomposed its row and filed 302,628 cycles under
"the returns every transcript hands back, by design". That was a true
statement about *why* those cycles were emulated and an unexamined one about
*whether they had to be*, and the convention turned out to be a habit. **A
transcript can end past its own `RTS`.** Three things had to hold and all
three did:

- **The core does not know what routine a transcript was entered at.** Nothing
  relates `resume_logical_pc` to the entry address, at the install site or at
  a checkpoint -- the core assigns it to `PC` and restarts its loop. The
  host's one related check is a consistency check: the reported bank must be
  what `output_registers.mpr[resume >> 13]` maps that segment to
  (`pce_runtime_beetle.cpp:2925`), so a walk resolves the bank through its own
  MPRs instead of assuming its own module's.
- **The return address is data the entry already carries.** The stack is
  ordinary work RAM at `$2100`-`$21FF`. `RTS` pops the low byte from
  `$2100 + S + 1` and the high from `$2100 + S + 2` and lands on that word
  plus one, `JSR` having pushed the address of its own last byte.
- **Interrupt delivery does not move.** The final checkpoint samples at its
  declared offset, advances to its end, assigns the caller's address and pops
  the frame -- all before the loop reaches `DcSelectInterrupt`. The boundary
  after the absorbed `RTS` is a real boundary with the caller's address in
  `PC` and `S` already popped, which is exactly what the machine does.

`RTS` is 6 cycles plus the one `LastCycle` charges after it samples: 21 master
with the interrupt sampled 3 back, so it needs no special `sample_back`. And
it **emits no write** -- which is what makes this provable rather than merely
plausible, because absorbing one is not allowed to move anything in any trace.

Nothing moved. All three golden artifacts held in the family regression, the
whole-registry census stayed `9036a9de...`, and an independent **Debug** run
of the same route reproduced the census, the work-RAM trace and the bus trace
byte-for-byte -- the determinism check the workflow requires when a change
touches interrupt-delivery machinery.

Measured on the palette family: **14,369 returns absorbed, +301,749 native
master cycles**, 671,640,741 -> 671,942,490, and `14,369 x 21` closes it
exactly. The seven return addresses fell from 302,628 emulated cycles to
**63** -- three executions reached by interpretation rather than through a
transcript -- and the row from 1,075,809 to 772,635:

| | Master cycles | Share | What it is |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| `00:EB46` | 625,095 | 80.9% | The whole-palette `TIA`, still the wall |
| `00:E94D` | 138,582 | 17.9% | The crossfade driver |
| the rest | 7,440 | 1.0% | Chunk boundaries and resumption |
| `00:EA77` | 1,455 | 0.2% | The fade-to-black driver |
| seven `RTS` | 63 | 0.008% | Three executions not absorbed |

One measured side effect, benign and to be expected wherever this is done
next. Nested installs rose 295,164 -> 295,258: extending a transcript by one
checkpoint means the instruction before the `RTS` no longer ends it, so there
is one more boundary at which an interrupt can arrive while the transcript is
still active, and its handler nests. Delivery lands on the same boundary at
the same cycle either way, which is why nothing moved. Depth stayed 3 of a
permitted 4, nothing refused.

This strikes a claim `NATIVE_PORT_WORKFLOW.md` had carried for a long time:
that call and return boundaries are "one of the hybrid's own overheads, which
no amount of porting removes", 13.3M on this route. The observation that
`08:40DE`-`41AB` was four `JSR`s and an `RTS` around an already-native routine
stands. The conclusion drawn from it does not. The `JSR` half is the same
argument from the caller's side -- composition, which `01:CB48` has been doing
since it was written -- and needs a *ported caller*, so it goes family by
family rather than as a sweep.

### Previous: asking the same question of the palette-shadow row

The answer was mostly negative -- which was worth as much as the dispatcher's
was, for the opposite reason.

The question `### Next` set was whether the palette row, 1,079,289 master
cycles carried as "the two fade drivers and the whole-palette `TIA` arm,
blocked", was parked by the same sentence `00:E058` had been: a load on the
hardware page. Disassembling the drivers and the arm answered it in one pass.
**There is not one load on the hardware page anywhere in `00:E93C`-`EBD6`.**
`00:EB30` drives the VCE and every access it makes is a store; the drivers and
the shadow routines never leave work RAM. The classification that unparked the
dispatcher -- outside input, device state a `peek` could carry, or a read that
changes the device -- has nothing here to sort.

Measuring the row per instruction says what it is made of instead:

| | Master cycles | Share | What it is |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| `00:EB46` | 625,095 | 58% | The whole-palette `TIA`. One instruction, 29 executions |
| six `RTS` | 302,628 | 28% | The returns every transcript here stops in front of, by design |
| `00:E94D`, `00:EA77` | 140,037 | 13% | The two fade drivers |
| the rest | 11,529 | 1% | `00:EAA7`'s chunk boundaries, and interrupt resumption |

**The `TIA` is a capacity wall, and it is also the cost.** 1,024 writes against
a 512-write channel, and a block transfer has no interior instruction boundary
for a chunk to stop at, so it will not move. The arm around it is ordinary, so
it splits the way the dispatcher did: `00:EB30` walks the four flag tests and
both colour-table stores and stops in front of the transfer, the core executes
it, `00:EB4D` clears `$2BB9` and `$2CCB` after it. `00:EB30` is admitted on all
3,599 calls now; the deployed registry goes 368 -> 369 routines and
671,636,826 -> 671,640,741 native cycles. That is **+3,915**, because the six
instructions the split moved are 2,523 cycles against the transfer's 625,095.

**So this bought admission, not cycles, and the contrast is the finding.** At
`00:E058` the unportable instruction was 17% of its block and the ordinary code
around it was the rest; here it is 99.6% of its arm. Reading a wall as an
instruction is always the right reading -- it is what turns a 29-call exception
into a clean registry row whose regression can state one invariant -- but the
slice has to be priced on what is either side of the instruction, not on the
row's total. The workflow now says so.

**A quarter of the row was never blocked at all.** 302,628 cycles are `RTS`
instructions the transcripts deliberately hand back. An inventory row that
counts emulated addresses counts them; no reading of "blocked" covers them.
*(This paragraph stopped one step short: it explained why those cycles were
emulated and never asked whether they had to be. The slice above absorbs them,
and the row's returns are now 63 cycles rather than 302,628.)*

**And the fade drivers get a third verdict.** They are reachable: the old note
that calling the frame-sync spin at `00:E321` forces a transcript across
twenty-one frames is wrong in the same way the dispatcher's note was wrong -- a
walk stops in front of the `JSR` and the return address is the next entry
point, and `00:E94D`'s own `TII $27B9, $27BA, $03FF` at `00:E950` (1,023 writes,
18,465 cycles) splits identically. They are left emulated because the route
enters `00:E94D` **once** and `00:EA77` eight times. Every entry point in this
family is admitted on hundreds or thousands of calls, which is what lets the
regression claim a transcript is state-generic rather than a transcription of
the one path observed. **Too few calls to prove anything is a decline, not a
block**, and writing it down as "blocked" is what sends the next reader to
re-survey a row with no answer left in it.

The census is `9036a9de...` unchanged and so are the work-RAM and bus write
traces. The bus trace is the sharp check here: the two `STZ` stores the split
moved into a transcript go to `$0402` and `$0403`, inside the traced VCE range,
so their values, order and master-cycle offsets are pinned against assembly.
405/405 Release in 164.88 s, 38/38 ROM-free Debug.

### Previous: asking whether `00:E058` is still blocked

The answer was no, for a reason nobody had written down, and both sides of the
one instruction that *is* blocked are now native.

The survey `### Next` asked for was whether the VDC gaining a native model
lifted the rule that parked the interrupt dispatcher. It did not — and the
rule was never the binding constraint. Two separate things had been rolled
into one sentence:

- **The value.** `PceVdc::read` already takes a `peek` flag that answers
  without disturbing anything, so the status byte could have been handed over
  on `RoutineEntry` exactly the way the frame's pad state is. This half did
  dissolve when the model landed, four slices ago, and nobody noticed.
- **The side effect.** Reading `$0000` clears every latched status source and
  is the only way the VDC's interrupt line falls. The replacement contract is
  a **write** channel; a write to `$0000` selects a register rather than
  acknowledging one. A transcript that predicted the byte and skipped the read
  would hand the core back an interrupt that had never been taken, and the
  handler would be re-entered immediately. This half does not lift, and it is
  the real answer.

**And it is a fact about one instruction, which the row had recorded as a
routine.** `LDA $0000` is one of nineteen instructions in the dispatcher, and
769,938 master cycles sat on the blocked list on its account. Above it are four
register saves that touch only the stack page; below it the byte the dispatcher
branches on is already in the accumulator, put there by a load the core
performed itself, so the device is never wanted again. `00:E058` walks to the
read and stops; the core executes it, at its own cycle, with its acknowledge
intact; `00:E05F` picks the dispatch up and hands off to whichever arm `$54`
selects.

Both are admitted on all 7,198 arrivals — 3,599 VBlank and 3,599 raster —
for **640,374 master cycles**, leaving 129,564 for the instruction itself.
The deployed registry moves from 366 routines and 670,996,452 native cycles to
368 and 671,636,826: 51.97% of the route, **94.53% of it outside the
frame-sync wait**. The state census is `9036a9de...` unchanged, and so are the
work-RAM and bus write traces — which is the stronger check, because the whole
stack page is in that trace and the four pushes now come from a transcript, so
their values, order and master-cycle offsets are pinned against assembly rather
than merely their end state.

**This needed no new capability, and that is the part worth keeping.** The
execution and replacement hooks fire in `RunSub` at every instruction boundary,
before the opcode fetch, so any ROM address is a legal entry point. `00:E05F`
is not a jump target and nothing in the game ever branches to it. That freedom
has been there since patch `0001`; what was missing was the question.

One small change to the shared walk: it now also stops when it reaches another
entry point in its own family, so the dispatcher's tail hands `00:E136` and
`00:E0EB` over as their own transactions instead of swallowing them and
emptying their rows in the registry census.

Modes 1, 2 and 5 of `$54` dispatch to `00:E0D0`, `00:E09E` and `00:E085`, which
this walk does not cover, so those branch targets decline the whole transaction
and stay emulated. None occurs on the census route: of the 3,599 VBlank
entries, 2,748 are mode 0 and 851 are mode 3.

### Previous: taking ownership of the controller port

The eighth entry on the fork boundary, and the census reproduces exactly either
way.

Patch `0019` adds the eighth entry on the fork boundary and the sixth device
model, but it is a different kind of slice from the five device models before
it: **nothing computed moved.** The strobe protocol this port speaks has been
native since phase 1, inside the cartridge's own pad reader at `00:E195`. What
it read *through* was still the emulator's chain — a frontend button buffer,
five `PCE_Input_Device` objects, a multitap counter — and that chain is what
this replaces. `devils_crush::input::PcePad` is two strobe lines, a read
counter and five devices; the host hands it an `InputFrame` and it holds it
until the machine's own `INPUT_Frame` latch, so *when* a device sees a press
is still the machine's decision.

**The acceptance is stronger than a matching census, and that is the point of
the slice.** For the sound and video models a silent fallback would have
produced the same census as the model, which is why those tests had to prove
the model was the default arm. Here the host starves the alternative: while a
pad model is installed the libretro input callback answers zero for every
query, so the emulator's own path is dead rather than merely bypassed. The
route reproduces `9036a9de...` anyway. Feeding the model nothing instead — the
same binary, one line changed — gives `24b1614f...`, a route where the game
never starts, which is what makes the match evidence rather than a
coincidence. The model also counts the thing directly: **540 of its 35,991
reads answered with a button held.**

What the route drives and what it does not is measured on the PSG's pattern.
Every read went through the multitap and none straight to the first port;
17,996 answered the button half and 17,995 the direction half; the counter was
reset 3,599 times and stepped 17,995; the half-selector toggled 17,995 times
and the six-button read path it selects ran **zero** times, because a
two-button host never sets the bit that reaches it. Neither filter removed
anything. The port is latched twice per frame — the emulator's frame loop runs
`INPUT_Frame` again after each mid-frame resynchronisation, which on this
machine is once — and reset twice in the route.

One asymmetry worth stating, because it is the first seam with it. Five ports
exist and two carry a host player, so three of them are permanently empty and
the model answers for them as an empty port rather than pretending they are
not there. A port carrying a mouse or the Tsushin keyboard would be answered
the same way, which would be *wrong* — so `configure_port` counts those as
unmodelled, `--report-pad-coverage` prints the count, and `dc_rom_native_pad`
fails on a nonzero one. The model does not model those devices and says so
rather than quietly standing in for them.

### Previous: fast-forwarding the frame-sync spin

Patch `0018` adds the seventh entry on the fork boundary and the first that is
a **capability** rather than a replacement: it takes no work away from the
emulator and computes nothing on its behalf. With no model registered the
machine is the machine it was, and the census reproduces `9036a9de...` to
prove it.

The split is the design. *Whether `00:E323` is a spin that changes nothing* is
a claim about a cartridge and lives in `devils_crush::cpu::HuC6280IdleSkip`.
*How far the machine may be advanced while nothing executes* is a claim about
the machine and lives in the fork.

The predicate verifies rather than believes. It reads the four bytes at the
watched address every time it is asked — `C5 zz` / `F0 FC`, a compare against
zero page and a branch that lands back on it — takes the zero-page address out
of the verified operand instead of being told it, and answers "idle" only
while the accumulator equals what that operand names. A wrong address, a bank
switch, or a ROM differing by one byte answers "not idle" and executes.

Over the census route it refuses **nothing** across 3,171,424 arrivals,
recognises exactly the **3,567** waits the survey counted, and skips
**21,077,517 of 24,248,940** iterations — 86.9%, nine per skip and 41 at most.
The route reproduces `9036a9de...` with the capability installed and with
`--emulated-idle` handing it back. Debug reproduces the same census and the
same coverage to the unit -- 3,171,424 arrivals, 21,077,517 iterations, 41 at
most -- so the skip is not a build-specific quantity.

The instruction boundary's own coverage is the sharpest evidence that nothing
but time was removed. Every counter describing what the boundary *decided* is
identical either way -- 1 reset, 254,990 timer vectors, 63,135 of them on a
line the latch did not hold, 7,198 IRQ1, 199,168 samples that latched a line,
7,213,928 behind the I flag, 2,008,130 woken and declined. Only the raw
per-instruction totals move, and by exactly the right amount: 108,732,259
decisions become 66,577,225, a difference of 42,155,034, which is two
instructions for each of the 21,077,517 skipped iterations and not one more.
`verify_native_boundary.cmake` therefore floors its "a route's worth of
instructions" check at sixty million rather than a hundred.

**The bound has two halves and only the first was obvious.** The horizon is
the first: advance whole iterations that end *strictly before* the scheduler's
near horizon, never up to it, so the crossing is left to a real instruction
and the placement of an event relative to an instruction boundary stays the
machine's decision.

The second cost a census to find. **Nothing may be standing either.** A
request the mask already admits has not been *latched* yet; the decision at
the top of the instruction loop reads the latch, so it answers "next
instruction" and the spin looks idle — but the next instruction's own
end-of-cycle sample would catch that request, and the boundary after it would
take the vector. A skip spans both boundaries and delivers the interrupt a
turn late, which is exactly what the first working version did: inside one
`00:E321` call the ordered writes stayed identical in sequence, value and
instruction address, and the interrupt entry landed 24 master cycles late.
`(IRQlow & IRQMask) != 0` is the whole fix, and it costs 1,452 skipped
iterations out of 21 million.

Two explanations were eliminated first, and both are worth keeping because
both pointed at the wrong mechanism. Granularity and the omitted
end-of-instruction samples: replacing the single advance with a per-iteration
replay of the exact `ADDCYC(3)`/sample/`ADDCYC(1)` pairs produces a
byte-identical census to the coarse skip, diverging the same way. And
proximity to the horizon: a whole iteration of slack diverges too,
differently. Both read as exonerating the sampling, and they do — the fault
was in the *deciding*. `LastCycle` latches once per instruction, but
`DcSelectInterrupt` runs once per pass of the instruction loop, and a skip
spans as many of those passes as it covers. A replay reproducing every sample
and every cycle still reproduces no decisions, which is why the fine and
coarse versions failed identically: a result that reads as exoneration and is
really a fingerprint.

One methodological note, since it wasted a cycle. Counting skips after which
`next_event` had gone non-positive returns zero, but that test cannot fail:
`reach_horizon` recalculates the horizon to a fresh positive value before the
advance returns, so a crossing is invisible to any test made after it.

### Previous: the parts of the sound chip the game never plays

The census proved the PSG device model on everything Devil's
Crush asks the chip to do, which is most of the chip and not all of it. The
model now counts its own paths, so `--report-psg-coverage` says exactly how
much: over the census route the waveform path emits 7,048,794 times and the
silent path 470,150, both across all six channels; the noise LFSR emits
824,410 times but **only on channel 5**; the accumulating output mode emits
**seven** times in an hour of frames; and the LFO runs **zero** times.

The plan's remedy for that was a second censused route, one that plays looping
music. It was the wrong instrument, and the ROM says so. The sequencer at
`45:4142` writes `$0809` from `$2E41`, and every write in the cartridge that
names that byte writes a zero into it: the cold start's `STZ $2E41` at
`45:4AB19`, and the sequencer's own `STA $2E41` at `45:4A20A`, which stores
back the value it has just masked the high bit out of. Nothing gives the byte
a value. (That is every absolute and absolute-indexed store whose target can
reach `$2E40`/`$2E41`; it does not rule out a bulk block transfer across work
RAM, but the sequencer reloads the register from that byte every frame and
the route reads `$00` on all 3,605 of them.) Another route would report the
same zero. A route is an oracle for what the game does; it is silent about
what the hardware does.

The oracle for the rest is the emulator's own device, driven directly.
`PCE_PSG` needs nothing from the machine around it — two buffers and a
revision to construct, a timestamp per call — so
`third_party/beetle-pce-fork/src/dc_beetle_reference_psg.cpp` exposes it as a
bare reference device and `tests/psg_device_tests.cpp` runs both chips from the
same synthetic register stream. After every scenario it compares not only the
two output buffers, position by position, but the entire device state: every
counter, waveform entry, sample latch, shift register and attenuation. Nine
scenarios and three seeded random streams, each against both chip revisions,
reach the LFO at all three depths and both ways the mixer turns it back off,
noise on channels 4 and 5 across all 32 periods, the accumulating mode on all
six channels either side of the cutoff, the volume walk, direct digital audio,
power and the frame rebase. It passed on the first run, both revisions.

A test is worth what it can catch, so it was checked the way the device was.
Perturbing the LFO shift by one fails the oscillator scenario *and* all three
random streams. Perturbing the accumulating mode's midpoint by one fails the
accumulating scenario on the HuC6280A and nowhere else — which is the revision
that subtracts it. And because agreement is only worth its coverage, the test
asserts its own path counters are non-zero, so a scenario that quietly stopped
reaching a path fails instead of passing.

This test lives exactly as long as the emulator does. What it leaves behind is
the record that the model was right while there was still something to be
right against — and the shape of the answer for the VDC, where the same split
will apply: the census for what the game drives, the emulator for what it
does not.

**The headline number was never a work queue.** Crossing a call is an edit to
a *transcript*; it is only available where a native walk already ends in front
of the call. Three different things put a `JSR` row in that bucket and only one
of them is a crossing:

- **A walk stops in front of it.** This was the only crossable case, and the
  profile could never tell you which rows they were — only
  `is_stop_instruction` could, because that is where the condition is written
  down. The sweep is empty now, so every surviving row is one of the two
  below.
- **The walk declines and the whole routine runs interpreted, call sites and
  all.** Bank `45`'s 476,490 is this, and it was recommended here last slice as
  the densest cluster to take first. `45:408F`, `45:4138`, `45:40AA` and
  `45:409F` have been crossings in `native_replacements_music.cpp` for slices;
  the rows are the tick's declined entries, 6,516 of 7,724 at `45:4044` alone,
  under the `$F5`/`$F7`/`$F9` guard against the timer driver's writes. The way
  to recover them is to widen admission, not to edit a call that is already an
  edit.
- **The code was never ported.** Bank `00`'s call bucket was 97,842 and is
  20,622 now, and the whole of the difference is the six `JSR`s the motion step
  crossed -- none of which appeared in any family source before it was written.
  Bank `01`'s 711,918 is unchanged and is the same story waiting to happen:
  `01:C154` and the `01:C16C`-`C18D` run. Crossing one on its own recovers 21
  cycles and leaves the body interpreted, which means porting the routine is
  the slice and the call comes free with it.

One grep per candidate settles which it is. That is now the third caution in
`docs/NATIVE_PORT_WORKFLOW.md`.

**The crossing technique was not finished after all, and the reason is worth
keeping.** It was recorded here as finished because the sweep it was built on --
every family's `is_stop_instruction`, filtered to ROM opcodes `$20` and `$44` --
returned nothing: no walk in the port ended in front of a call. That was true,
and it stayed true for exactly as long as no new walk was written. The substep loop
crossed eight calls and the motion step six more, all fourteen in code that had
no walk at all until it was ported. **A crossing is not a technique you exhaust;
it is what a walk does when it meets a call, so the supply of them is the supply
of unported code.** The motion step added a second case to it: four of its six
crossings went to leaves the same slice owns, so the call and the body on the
far side of it were converted together. The preamble after it added a third
case that is not a crossing at all -- it ends by falling through into a
registered address, which converts no call and pays nothing for the hand-off.

**The `JSR` bucket is still not crossable as it stands, and for the same two
reasons.** A row is in it because the routine around it declines and runs
interpreted, or because nobody has ported it. Neither is fixed by editing the
call. `03:7F5D` (63,987) is *composed* inline by the collision module and its
row is the declined path; `03:652B`, `03:6528`, `03:649C`, `03:6499` (55-59k
each) and `02:5EEC` (44,919) appear in no family source at all. Those are ports,
and the calls come free with them -- which is exactly what happened to bank
`00`'s six rows, and to `01:C73F`, `01:C749` and `01:C75E` the slice before,
every one of them listed here under "the code was never ported" and collected
by porting the code around it.

be guarded host-side.

**Two of the three runs this list recommended last slice were not routines.**
It offered `09:71EA`-`09:7247` (245,358) and `09:725E`-`09:72EA` (164,607) as
separate candidates. They are two fragments of one routine, `09:7237`, which
branches over an untaken countdown so that the analyzer's contiguous-address
grouping puts a hole in the middle of it. Read as a unit it was 327,924 and it
became this slice. **The analyzer's runs are address ranges; disassemble before
pricing.** The remaining fragments of those two runs are `09:71EA`-`720A`
(45,000, an animation frame stepper, and `09:70C1`-`70E4` is a near-identical
second copy worth 44,703) and `09:727D`-`72EA` (33,987, the tail of the redraw
this slice's poll now guards).

**Taken.** `09:72FD`-`09:737B` was the one candidate from that list that *is* a
routine and was the largest single routine left anywhere: **284,361 master
cycles, 63% of what remains in bank `09`**, 376 calls, fifty-six instructions
and not one branch. It is the score panel's glyph writer -- the leaf the redraw
calls once per digit. Three things are already known about it:

- **It is a device routine**, and that is the point of taking it. It selects VDC
  register 0, writes a VRAM address from `$35`/`$36`, selects register 2, and
  pushes four tile words from the table at `$7390` indexed by `A * 4`, stepping
  the address by `$40` between the two rows and back by `$42` at the end -- a
  net two columns *backwards*, because the panel is drawn right to left from the
  least significant digit.
- **The machinery for it exists and is proven.** `$0000`-`$0003` is already in
  `is_replaceable_hardware_port`, and `native_replacements_vram.cpp` prices a
  `STA $0003` at 18 master cycles sampling at `- 6` throughout -- the stealing
  port's last cycle lands after `LastCycle`, so it is the `- 6` case, not `- 3`.
- **Do not price it from the profile.** Two of its rows, `09:732E` and `09:736A`,
  average 33.8 master cycles against 18 for the same instruction at four other
  addresses. Those two are the second `$0003` write of each pair, which completes
  a VRAM word and stalls until the VDC yields a slot. The core charges that stall
  on the checkpointed path, so the transcript declares 18 and the credited gain
  will be materially below 284,361. Measure it, do not assume it.

It also reads ROM -- `$7390,Y` through MPR3 -- which twenty-four replacements
already do; `native_replacements_vblank.cpp` has the `read_rom` lambda to copy.

All 376 calls now execute natively and every call, work-RAM write, and VDC bus
write matches assembly. The declared gain is 270,720 master cycles; the other
13,641 are dynamic VDC arbitration stalls still charged by the real device.
The re-profile leaves 169,008 emulated master cycles in bank `09`, so that bank
is no longer a useful unit to optimize. The subsequent Spider-parent slice
removes bank `03`'s two largest complete runs and leaves 532,035 there. Select
the next slice by bounding the largest live non-entry runs in banks `02` and
`01`, starting with `02:523F-526A`; do not port an address row until its
enclosing routine and any declined parent are known.

After bank `09`, the cheap work is the fifty jump-table rows in bank `01` that
this route never reaches, whenever a route reaches them.

turned out to be nine times the largest row in it — rank by what the machine
executes, not by what the technique of the moment can absorb.

Bank `03` is the largest pool again and has had thirty edits already, but read
its two biggest rows before starting. `03:6A37` + `03:6988` at 176,025 are
*residue* on a routine that already absorbs at its entry wrapper -- transcripts
an interrupt cut short, plus arrivals through the three sites that call the
interpreter in line and by design never absorb. Both kinds are cycles the
assembly genuinely runs, so nothing recovers them short of shortening the
transcripts or transcribing the compositions differently. The fork patch was
guessed at as a way in and is not one; that was settled by measuring, and both
rows are unmoved. Everything below them in bank `03` is unported parents.

**What is left is mostly not absorbable, and the rows say so.** Of the
1,562,493 remaining, `03`'s 176,025 is residue, `03:603E` at 137,607 and
`03:7F80` at 94,878 are an unported parent and an untranscribed arm, and
`00:E32B` at 75,123 is the frame-sync waiter's own return -- reachable only by
registering `00:E327` as an entry of its own, which is the one cheap row still
standing. Below those it is unported parents in the 14k-60k range. The next
comparable win is more likely to be a routine nobody has ported than a return
nobody has absorbed.

**Look for a stop list first.** It is the cheapest thing in this technique and
it has now paid five times: bank `01`'s two walking interpreters were 372,411
between them, bank `00`'s call wrappers were 475,071 in a single edit, and bank
`45`'s music sequencer was 575,916 in one condition. Grep for
`is_stop_instruction` and `is_return_instruction` to see which families already
have the shape. Then read the list rather than counting it -- check the opcode
at every stop against the ROM, and check what each `RTS` actually pops.

**Check where each stop leaves the stack pointer.** Bank `00` is the reason
this is now a step of its own. A wrapper written in two halves returns above
where its second half was entered, and `absorb_return` wants the pointer *at
the return*. Give each stop a pop count rather than testing it for equality
with the entry, and derive the count from pushes and pops the walk models so a
disagreement stays a modelling error worth refusing on.

**If a write trace grows without bound, the routine is the wrong thing to
watch.** A routine entered by an `RTS` landing and returning above its entry
has no `RTS` at its own depth for the observer to close on, so the call it
opens never closes. Watch the head that opened the call instead, which is what
`OBSERVE` is for.

**Rank by ported owner, not by cycles**, and the seven banks done so far
bracket what that means: bank `03` took eight edits for 1,054,221 because its
pool was spread, then twenty-two more for 873,453 because two of its rows were
shared routines; bank `08` took two for 1,633,611 because 95% of it was two
returns of already-native walks; bank `02` took twenty-one for 1,314,528 and was
both at once; bank `01` took twenty-one for 872,514; bank `00` took six for
694,653 because four of its six families already ended at a fixed set of
addresses; bank `45` took **one** for 575,916 because all of it was a single
walk that already did. No number in the table above predicts any of that.

The last column is a crude discriminator run over the whole profile in one
pass: for each non-entry `RTS` row, ask whether its address appears anywhere in
`src/app/*.cpp` as a hexadecimal literal. It over-counts -- a mention can be a
resume address, a branch target or a `return_instruction` on an arm that hands
over mid-routine rather than one a walk ends on. Bank `00` demonstrated both
directions: it read 705,303 mentioned before that slice and delivered 694,653,
and what is left reads only 10,650, which is honest. Bank `45` is now the
counter-example to trusting it downward as well as upward: 54,438 of its
remaining 68,481 still reads as mentioned, and almost none of that is
absorbable -- it is residue on stops the walk does end at but did not reach on
those arrivals.

**The other thing `### Next` could be is the fork patch.** `01:C510` is the
only family so far that cannot absorb, and the reason is a host limitation
rather than anything about the routine: a transaction stages its absorbed
return when it is installed and nothing withdraws the promise when the
transcript is cut short, so a routine re-entered at the same stack depth
redeems a stale one against a live call. The core knows when it abandons a
transcript -- `ReplacementActive` goes false in eight places in
`patches/0006-huc6280-interruptible-replacement.patch` -- so the patch is a
callback from there into `pending_absorbed_returns_`. It is worth 73,536 cycles
at `01:C52B` directly, and more in what it unblocks: every family from here on
that is long and re-entrant is in the same position, and there is no way to
tell from the profile which those are.

What to carry across rather than rediscover:

- **Read the family's regression before changing its walk.** Not for the stack
  page -- for what it observes. This is the step that turned up the broken call
  trace three slices ago, and the step that turned up the stale Debug baseline
  the slice before.
- **Prove it by comparison, not by hash.** Trace the family emulated and
  replaced and require the census, the call trace and the call-write trace to
  be byte-identical. A recorded expectation can drift into agreeing with a
  mistake; the emulated run cannot. This has now caught a host bug in two of
  the last four slices, both on the first family it was pointed at, and in a
  third it caught a four-slice-old write-cycle error at `02:5408` that the
  family's own recorded hash had been agreeing with all along.
- **When the comparison does differ, find out whose bug it is before fixing
  it.** Rebuild with the absorption removed and run the replaced trace again.
  If it matches the emulated one, the difference is this slice's; if it does
  not, the slice has found something older and the fix belongs somewhere else.
  Two builds and two runs, and it is the difference between a fix and a guess.
  Bank `45` is the case where it mattered and nothing was wrong: three of its
  fifteen entries differed, the removal build reproduced the difference
  byte-for-byte, and the slice was clean.
- **A loop head cannot be compared call-for-call, and that is not a fault.**
  An entry reached by a `JMP` from inside its own body -- `45:4044`, `45:409C`,
  `45:4143`, each closing a loop -- opens a fresh call on every arrival when the
  route is emulated, but one transcript swallows all the arrivals it runs
  through. The replaced trace is a strict subset of the emulated one, not a
  match: at `45:4143`, 9,602 calls against 19,062, every one of the 9,602
  present verbatim. Check the subset relation rather than the hash, and check
  it in that direction -- a replaced call *absent* from the emulated trace is
  the real fault this would otherwise hide.
- **Look for a stop list before ranking rows.** A walking interpreter that ends
  in front of whichever address in a fixed list it reached is one absorption for
  the whole family, however many registered entries dispatch it -- and it is the
  only case where the rows have to be *read* rather than counted. A stop list
  mixes returns with mid-routine handovers and with `RTS` instructions that are
  not returns at all. `01:CBF9` pushes a vector and lets the `RTS` jump to it;
  absorbing there would have computed the right landing address and still
  reported a completed call where none completed. Check the opcode at every
  stop, then check what each `RTS` actually pops.
- **Check where each stop leaves the stack pointer; it is not always the
  entry's.** Bank `00`'s call wrappers are written in two halves around the
  call they exist to make, and the second half returns above where it was
  entered -- `00:E261` two bytes up on `00:E241`'s frame, `00:ECF1` three up on
  `00:ECC6`'s. `absorb_return`'s stack-pointer argument has always meant the
  pointer *at the return*; every family before `01:C5C9` merely had the two
  equal. Give each stop a pop count rather than testing it for equality with
  the entry, and derive the count from pushes and pops the walk models so a
  disagreement stays a modelling error worth refusing on.
- **A routine that returns above its entry cannot be watched.** The observer
  opens a call at the entry pointer and closes it on the next `RTS` standing
  there; for a tail like `00:ECE2` there is none, so the call never closes and
  collects the rest of the route's writes -- the trace passed twenty gigabytes
  before it was stopped. That is the instrument, not the routine. Watch the
  head that opened the call: `verify_absorbed_return_trace.cmake` takes an
  `OBSERVE` argument for exactly this, and if a write trace grows without bound
  this is the first thing to check.
- **A promise the transcript never keeps has to be withdrawn, and only the core
  knows when.** A transaction stages its absorbed return when it is *installed*,
  and the observer redeems it at the boundary the machine lands on afterwards.
  A transcript the core gives up on never lands, and the promise used to stay
  queued -- harmless until the routine is re-entered at the same stack depth, at
  which point it finds a live call and closes it with an abandoned transcript's
  registers: correct cycles, wrong `Y` and `MPR`. Fixed by
  `patches/0020-huc6280-replacement-abandonment.patch`, which hands the host
  back a token naming the transcript. If you write another transcript that
  *declares* something rather than merely replacing work, this is the seam that
  has to know about it.
- **A guess about where a limitation bites is worth measuring before it is
  worth acting on.** The stale promise was recorded as also holding back bank
  `03`'s two biggest rows. It was not: those 176,025 cycles are residue on a
  routine that already absorbs, and the patch left both rows exactly where they
  were. One profile run settled it. A limitation that explains one symptom is
  not thereby the explanation of every symptom that resembles it.
- **A shared routine absorbs at its entry, not inside itself.** If any other
